XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. 'Go, Elfyn, go': dyna oedd y gri wythnos yma ym mhentref Dinas Mawddwy, ac ar hyd a lled Cymru y benwythnos hon. Wrth i genedl gyfan ddal eu gwynt, croesi bysedd a gwylio pob car a phob cornel, daeth y freuddwyd yn realiti yn haul Sardinia: Elfyn Evans a Scott Martin, pencampwyr ralio’r byd. Llongyfarchiadau iddynt. Ac am ddiweddglo. Ar ôl blynyddoedd o ddod mor agos—ar ôl boddi wrth y lan dro ar ôl tro ar ôl tro—am bleser oedd hi o’r diwedd gweld Elfyn yn codi’r tlws arbennig, a hynny o dan yr amgylchiadau mwyaf dramatig posib.

A thra mor felys fu’r fuddugoliaeth, am wych oedd gweld y ddrama’n datblygu’n fyw ar S4C, gan ganiatáu i genedl gyfan rannu’r cyffro, y nerfau a’r dathlu drwy gyfrwng y Gymraeg. 'Drama yn y diwedd' ebychodd sylwebydd Ralio, Howard Davies, geiriau sydd bellach wedi eu clywed ledled y byd.

Llongyfarchiadau mawr, Elfyn, Cymro a'r Prydeiniwr cyntaf i gyflawni’r gamp ers chwarter canrif. Rydym i gyd mor falch o dy lwyddiant haeddiannol—neb llai, wrth gwrs, na dy dad, Gwyndaf, yntau’n gyn-bencampwr rali Prydain, ac sydd wedi dy ddilyn ar hyd y daith. O Ddinas Mawddwy i binacl y byd—am stori, am dymor, ac am fuddugoliaeth. Y Cymro balch o wlad y Gwylliaid bellach yn bencampwr y byd. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Thank you, Llywydd. 'Go, Elfyn, go': that was the chant this week in the village of Dinas Mawddwy, and all over Wales this weekend. As a whole nation held its collective breath, crossed its fingers and watched every car and every corner, the dream became a reality in the Sardinian sun: Elfyn Evans and Scott Martin, world rally champions. Congratulations to them. And what a finale. After years of coming so close—falling just short time and time again—what a pleasure it was to finally see Elfyn lift up this special trophy, and to do so under the most dramatic circumstances possible.

And while the victory was so sweet, how wonderful it was to see the drama unfold live on S4C, which allowed the entire nation to share the excitement, the nerves and the celebrations through the medium of Welsh. 'Drama at the finishing line' was the exclamation of the Ralio commentator, Howard Davies, words that have now reverberated around the world.

Congratulations, Elfyn, the first Welshman and Briton to achieve this feat in a quarter of a century. We're all so proud of your well-deserved success—none more so, of course, than your own father, Gwyndaf, a former British rally champion, who has followed you all along this journey. From Dinas Mawddwy to the pinnacle of the world—what a story, what a season and what a victory. The proud Welshman from the land of the Gwylliaid, now the world champion. Thank you.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Today, I stand to remember the victims of the horrific attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023. We remember the 1,200 people who lost their lives. We remember the families torn apart, the communities devastated and all those who were taken hostage. And today, I particularly want to remember two little boys, Ariel and Kfir Bibas. You may remember Ariel, a beautiful young boy in his Batman outfit running through the streets, and I wear my badge in memory of him today and anyone lost in this attack. Ariel was just four years old when he was taken, and Kfir was only nine months old. Their faces became known around the world as a heartbreaking symbol of innocent lives caught up in the horror of that day. We remember their mother, Shiri, too. We think of their father, Yarden, and the unimaginable loss endured by the Bibas family.

Whatever our politics, there should always be space in this Chamber for humanity. There should be space to mourn innocent people, to condemn terrorism and to say clearly that deliberately targeting and taking civilian hostages can never be justified. So, today, from the Welsh Parliament, I, we, remember Ariel and Kfir and Shiri and Yarden and every innocent life taken on that day as a consequence. May their memories be a blessing and may all those who mourn find strength and peace.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Heddiw, rwy'n codi i gofio dioddefwyr yr ymosodiadau erchyll yn Israel ar 7 Hydref 2023. Rydym yn cofio'r 1,200 o bobl a gollodd eu bywydau. Rydym yn cofio'r teuluoedd a chwalwyd, y cymunedau a ddinistriwyd a phawb a gafodd eu cymryd yn wystlon. A heddiw, rwyf eisiau cofio dau fachgen bach, Ariel a Kfir Bibas. Efallai y byddwch chi'n cofio Ariel, bachgen ifanc prydferth yn ei wisg Batman yn rhedeg trwy'r strydoedd, ac rwy'n gwisgo fy mathodyn er cof amdano heddiw ac unrhyw un a gollwyd yn yr ymosodiad hwn. Pedair oed oedd Ariel pan gafodd ei gymryd, a dim ond naw mis oed oedd Kfir. Daeth eu hwynebau'n adnabyddus ledled y byd fel symbol torcalonnus o fywydau diniwed wedi'u dal yn arswyd y diwrnod hwnnw. Rydym yn cofio eu mam, Shiri, hefyd. Rydym yn meddwl am eu tad, Yarden, a'r golled anhygoel a ddioddefodd y teulu Bibas.

Beth bynnag yw ein gwleidyddiaeth, dylai fod lle bob amser yn y Siambr hon i ddynoliaeth. Dylai fod lle i alaru am bobl ddiniwed, i gondemnio terfysgaeth ac i ddweud yn glir na ellir cyfiawnhau targedu a chymryd gwystlon sifil yn fwriadol. Felly, heddiw, o Senedd Cymru, rwyf i, rydym ni'n cofio Ariel a Kfir a Shiri a Yarden a phob bywyd diniwed a gymerwyd ar y diwrnod hwnnw o ganlyniad. Boed i'r cof amdanynt fod yn fendith a boed i bawb sy'n galaru ddod o hyd i nerth a heddwch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 4. Datganiadau 90 eiliad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 4. 90-second Statements
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
This week is the first National Cadets Week, and I wanted to take the opportunity to recognise both the young people involved in the cadet forces and the volunteers who give up so much of their time to support them. I've been involved with the Royal Air Force Air Cadets for more than 40 years, first in uniform as a cadet and a member of staff, and now as a civilian trustee, so this is something very close to me.

Over those years, I've seen many young people come through the organisation. Some have gone on to join the armed forces, but many haven't, and that's not the point. What the cadet movement does particularly well is give young people opportunities; it gives them confidence, responsibility, friendships and experiences they might otherwise never have had. And none of this happens without the adult volunteers who turn up week after week, often after a full day's work, and give their evenings and weekends to make it happen. His Majesty the King has recognised their contribution during National Cadets Week, and I would simply like to add my thanks. After more than 40 years, I am still very proud to be involved. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Yr wythnos hon yw'r Wythnos Genedlaethol Cadetiaid gyntaf, ac roeddwn i eisiau manteisio ar y cyfle i gydnabod y bobl ifanc sy'n ymwneud â'r lluoedd cadetiaid a'r gwirfoddolwyr sy'n rhoi cymaint o'u hamser i'w cefnogi. Bûm yn ymwneud â Chadetiaid Awyr yr Awyrlu Brenhinol ers dros 40 mlynedd, yn gyntaf mewn lifrai fel cadet ac aelod o staff, a nawr fel ymddiriedolwr sifil, felly mae hyn yn rhywbeth sy'n agos iawn at fy nghalon.

Dros y blynyddoedd hynny, gwelais lawer o bobl ifanc yn dod trwy'r sefydliad. Mae rhai wedi mynd yn eu blaenau i ymuno â'r lluoedd arfog, ond mae yna lawer nad ydynt wedi gwneud hynny, ac nid dyna'r pwynt. Yr hyn y mae'r mudiad cadetiaid yn ei wneud yn arbennig o dda yw rhoi cyfleoedd i bobl ifanc; mae'n rhoi hyder, cyfrifoldeb, cyfeillgarwch a phrofiadau iddynt na fyddent wedi'u cael fel arall. Ac nid oes dim o hyn yn digwydd heb yr oedolion sy'n gwirfoddoli a ddaw yno wythnos ar ôl wythnos, yn aml ar ôl diwrnod llawn o waith, ac sy'n rhoi eu nosweithiau a'u penwythnosau i wneud iddo ddigwydd. Mae Ei Fawrhydi y Brenin wedi cydnabod eu cyfraniad yn ystod Wythnos Genedlaethol y Cadetiaid, a hoffwn ychwanegu fy niolch. Ar ôl mwy na 40 mlynedd, rwy'n dal i fod yn falch iawn o gymryd rhan. Diolch.

Just over 18 weeks ago, Venus Lamey turned up at the Nova Prestatyn parkrun dressed as a chicken. Since then, she has run 16 different parkruns across north Wales, dressed in a variety of costumes, including a dinosaur, a unicorn and Winnie the Pooh. Several of these parkruns have been in my constituency, Pont y Bala, Dolgellau and Hafan Pwllheli, where I went to meet her and to hear her story of why she chooses to run in some very eye-catching costumes. Venus believes in shifting shame. She runs because it helps her and to raise money for the Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Centre North Wales, who support the victims of sexual violence. Venus says, 'Through the hundreds of conversations I've had, it's highlighted to me just how many people in north Wales have either been affected by sexual violence themselves or know someone who has.'

Venus wants to shift the shame from the victims of sexual abuse to the perpetrators. Last week, she ran the Nova Prestatyn parkrun again, wearing a Teletubbies costume, but this time, she wasn't the only one in an embarrassing costume: 64 people dressed up for Venus's Shift the Shame campaign. Venus will run her final parkrun this Saturday on the prom at Abermaw—Barmouth. So, if you're in the area, do go and cheer her on. Diolch, Venus, for everything you do.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Ychydig dros 18 wythnos yn ôl, daeth Venus Lamey i parkrun Nova Prestatyn wedi'i gwisgo fel iâr. Ers hynny, mae hi wedi rhedeg 16 parkrun gwahanol ar draws gogledd Cymru wedi'i gwisgo mewn amrywiaeth o wisgoedd, gan gynnwys dinosor, uncorn a Winnie the Pooh. Mae sawl un o'r parkruns hyn wedi bod yn fy etholaeth i, Pont y Bala, Dolgellau a Hafan Pwllheli, pan euthum i'w chyfarfod ac i glywed ei stori pam ei bod yn dewis rhedeg mewn gwisgoedd trawiadol iawn. Mae Venus yn credu mewn symud baich cywilydd. Mae hi'n rhedeg am fod hynny'n ei helpu ac i godi arian ar gyfer Canolfan Gymorth Trais a Cham-drin Rhywiol Gogledd Cymru, sy'n cefnogi dioddefwyr trais rhywiol. Dywed Venus, 'Drwy'r cannoedd o sgyrsiau a gefais, mae wedi amlygu i mi faint o bobl yng ngogledd Cymru sydd naill ai wedi cael eu heffeithio gan drais rhywiol eu hunain neu sy'n adnabod rhywun a effeithiwyd ganddo.'

Mae Venus eisiau symud baich cywilydd oddi ar ddioddefwyr cam-drin rhywiol i'r troseddwyr. Yr wythnos diwethaf, rhedodd y parkrun Nova Prestatyn eto, gan wisgo gwisg Teletubbies, ond y tro hwn, nid hi oedd yr unig un mewn gwisg wirion: fe wisgodd 64 o bobl i fyny ar gyfer ymgyrch Shift the Shame Venus. Bydd Venus yn rhedeg ei parkrun olaf ddydd Sadwrn yma ar y prom yn Abermaw. Felly, os ydych chi yn yr ardal, ewch i'w chefnogi. Diolch, Venus, am bopeth rydych chi'n ei wneud.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Cynnig NDM9297 Tom Montgomery, Jane Dodds, Natasha Asghar, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd

Cefnogwyd gan Art Wright, Helen Jenner, Iain McIntosh, John Clark, Louise Emery

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn gresynu nad oes Llys Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol (FDAC) wedi bod yng Nghymru ers mis Tachwedd 2023.

2. Yn nodi argymhelliad 35 yn yr adroddiad Cyfiawnder yng Nghymru dros Bobl Cymru ym mis Hydref 2019, sef y dylid sefydlu Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol yng Nghymru.

3. Yn cydnabod yr argymhelliad yn adroddiad Gwerthusiad o Gynllun Peilot y Llys Cyffuriau ac Alcohol i Deuluoedd yng Nghymru ym mis Mawrth 2024, sef y dylai cynlluniau i ehangu FDAC ymhellach yng Nghymru gael eu datblygu.

4. Yn croesawu’r canfyddiadau o’r treial yng Nghymru:

a) bod rhieni yn hynod gadarnhaol ynghylch eu profiad o fod yn rhan o achos FDAC;

b) bod nifer y rhieni oedd yn camddefnyddio sylweddau ar ddechrau achos FDAC wedi gostwng o 83 y cant i 54 y cant; ac

c) bod nifer y plant oedd yng ngofal un neu’r ddau o’u rhieni wedi mwy na dyblu.

5. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i:

a) gweithredu’r argymhelliad i fwrw ymlaen â chreu FDACs ledled Cymru;

b) sicrhau bod FDACs yn rhan o strategaeth sy’n helpu i gadw plant allan o ofal; ac

c) dysgu o brofiad y 13 tîm FDAC arbenigol sy’n gweithredu ar hyn o bryd, sy'n gweithio mewn 18 llys ac yn cefnogi teuluoedd mewn 35 awdurdod lleol yn Lloegr.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Motion NDM9297 Tom Montgomery, Jane Dodds, Natasha Asghar, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd

Supported by Art Wright, Helen Jenner, Iain McIntosh, John Clark, Louise Emery

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Regrets that there has been no Family Drug and Alcohol Court (FDAC) in Wales since November 2023.

2. Notes recommendation 35 in the Justice in Wales for the People of Wales report from October 2019 that Family Drug and Alcohol Courts should be established in Wales.

3. Acknowledges the recommendation in the Evaluation of the Family Drug and Alcohol Court in Wales pilot report from March 2024 that plans to scale FDAC further in Wales should progress.

4. Welcomes the findings from the trial in Wales that:

a) parents were overwhelmingly positive about their experience of being involved in FDAC proceedings;

b) the number of parents misusing substances at the start of FDAC proceedings decreased from 83 per cent to 54 per cent; and

c) the number of children in the care of one or both of their parents more than doubled.

5. Calls on the Welsh Government to:

a) deliver on the recommendation to progress with creating FDACs across Wales;

b) ensure that FDACs form a part of a strategy that helps keep children out of care; and

c) learn from the experience of the 13 specialist FDAC teams currently in operation, working in 18 courts and supporting families in 35 local authorities in England.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Thank you, Llywydd. Before having the honour of being elected, I worked with some of the most vulnerable people in north Wales. As a Member of the Senedd, I have continued to champion their cause. Members, we should be deeply concerned that our country has a much higher rate of children in care than in England. In 2025, there were 114 children per 10,000 in the care of Welsh local authorities, compared to 67 children per 10,000 in the care of the local authorities in England. There are currently around 7,000 children in placement. In Wrexham, there are over 300 young people living in such a situation; Swansea has 475 and, in Cardiff, it's nearly 1,000.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Diolch, Lywydd. Cyn cael yr anrhydedd o gael fy ethol, gweithiais gyda rhai o'r bobl fwyaf agored i niwed yng ngogledd Cymru. Fel Aelod o'r Senedd, rwyf wedi parhau i hyrwyddo eu hachos. Aelodau, dylem fod yn bryderus iawn fod gan ein gwlad gyfradd lawer uwch o blant mewn gofal nag yn Lloegr. Yn 2025, roedd 114 o blant ym mhob 10,000 yng ngofal awdurdodau lleol Cymru, o'i gymharu â 67 o blant ym mhob 10,000 yng ngofal yr awdurdodau lleol yn Lloegr. Ar hyn o bryd mae tua 7,000 o blant wedi'u lleoli mewn gofal. Yn Wrecsam, mae dros 300 o bobl ifanc yn byw mewn sefyllfa o'r fath; mae gan Abertawe 475 ac yng Nghaerdydd, mae'r ffigur bron yn 1,000.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Daeth y Dirprwy Lywydd (Kerry Ferguson) i’r Gadair.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: The Deputy Presiding Officer (Kerry Ferguson) took the Chair.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
These figures are alarming, but they are not just numbers; they're human beings whose lives can be seriously impacted by their experience. Young people with care experience told the previous Senedd that, for example, some school teachers made it really obvious that they were in care, meaning that they never had a break from their experience of the care system. They told the previous Senedd that they had very little support to help them move on from foster placements and that they lacked the basic skills needed to live independently. 

We know that care leavers are underrepresented at universities and are on what Crisis describes as a 'predictable route' into homelessness. According to the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, they are approximately four times more likely to have a mental health need compared to children living with their birth families. Overwhelmingly, professionals and academics have made it clear that corporate parenting has not been achieving for care-experienced children and young people.

Parents are being failed too. Research shows that parents who go through care proceedings once are more likely to find themselves in proceedings again with subsequent children. Forty-seven per cent of newborn babies subject to care proceedings in England were born to mothers who had previously had children subject to care proceedings. The Nuffield Family Justice Observatory found that mothers and fathers who are frequently involved in care proceedings are dealing with complex and unresolved trauma, which is compounded by the court experience. The adversarial proceedings, formal language and impersonal process compound anxieties and triggers self-protective behaviours, which negatively impact the relationship between the professional and the family unit. Parents feel that they are not being listened to. As the independent review of children's social care in 2022 found, court proceedings are, by their nature, adversarial and have a high human and economic cost.

Members, it doesn't have to be like this. There is another way: family drug and alcohol courts. How are these different? I want to answer by quoting the words of a parent who had previously had children removed, comparing the FDAC process to the standard process. Of the standard process, she said, 'We felt like we had no voice and that we were powerless, and that we were just being accused of things and that there was no opportunity to defend ourselves.' Speaking of the family drug and alcohol court process, the same parent said, 'It feels like we have the power to actually have our say, get things done, have our side heard, and then they try to work with us to improve things and meet in the middle.'

Unlike standard proceedings, FDAC uses a trauma-informed approach, which includes listening to parents without judgment, focusing on parents' strengths and the resources that they currently have available to them, and allowing flexibility. Parents are given a key worker from the FDAC team and a judge who provides them with support and a problem-solving approach. There is weekly substance misuse testing, which involves the parents, and fortnightly non-lawyer reviews with consistent legal monitoring that creates a forum for judges and professionals to problem solve with the parents, set clear goals and delegate tasks for the following two weeks. Parents have a multidisciplinary team to support them, who help them to gain access to services and agencies. They provide transparent information and set up multiple sessions per week to address the intervention plan.

Clearly, it’s a very different model to the standard process, but how do we get families there? One challenge that arose from the Welsh trial was that the number of referrals was hampered by confusion over the threshold. Professionals were thought to be pre-screening referrals themselves and only referring if parents' substance misuse was particularly severe. Some legal representatives were under the impression that the local authority was responsible for determining which cases met the threshold, while the judge suggested that there was a general lack of awareness and exposure to the model.

That lack of awareness can be overcome when we follow the model used in London, which is that the usual threshold for proceedings applies, meaning that if a family is not selected for the model, they will enter the usual family proceedings court instead, and a family will qualify if they have a history of parental drug or alcohol misuse. So, now that we know what these courts are, I want to show you why the FDACs are a more effective model.

The evaluation of the family drug and alcohol court in Wales found that the number of parents misusing substances decreased from 83 per cent at the start of the process to 54 per cent. The number of parents misusing alcohol, thanks to the proceedings, reduced from 91 per cent to 60 per cent. Not perfect, but a marked improvement. The number of parents recorded as misusing drugs fell from 94 per cent to 51 per cent. Those supported by the experience of family drug and alcohol courts in England and, more recently, the national FDAC impact evaluation, found that a higher proportion of parents stopped misusing drugs or alcohol by the end of the proceedings. The pilot in Wales showed that the number of children in the care of one or both of their parents more than doubled from the start of the proceedings to the end. That is supported, again, by a study in England, which found that 52 per cent of children were returned to their parents, compared to only 13 per cent in the standard process. The family teams almost halved the number of children being placed in local authority care. That's more family units kept as one.

There are other proven benefits too. Unsurprisingly, feedback from parents is overwhelmingly positive. The Bedfordshire team evaluation saw parents describe the process as non-judgmental and inclusive, whilst parents in London described the system as transformative. And here in Wales, a parent who was reunited with their child at the end of the proceedings described the service as a lifesaver and said, 'My life's back on track because of the FDAC team. I can't recommend them enough.' 'I can't recommend them enough'—what a contrast to how parents feel about the standard process.

It is a serious failure that whilst England has 13 of these specialist teams, we don't have a single one in Wales. The current situation goes against recommendation 35 of the 'Justice in Wales for the People of Wales' report. It goes against the recommendation in the evaluation of the Welsh pilot. It goes against the best interests of children, young people and their parents. There is no reason why this injustice cannot be stopped. This is confirmed when also considering the economic case.

The Centre for Justice Innovation and Mutual Ventures' economic analysis shows that, for every £1 spent on FDAC operations, £3 is generated in savings to the taxpayer. A reduction in the cost of children's services needs to be taken extremely seriously, especially when we consider that overspends in Welsh local authorities arising from children's social care last year alone came to nearly £30 million. Bearing in mind the benefit to the taxpayer, the benefit to some of our most vulnerable children and the benefit to some of our most vulnerable parents, I urge the Senedd to back my motion today. Let us together create a care system that builds, not breaks families. Thank you.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Mae'r ffigurau hyn yn frawychus, ond nid rhifau yn unig ydynt; maent yn fodau dynol y gall eu profiad effeithio'n ddifrifol ar eu bywydau. Dywedodd pobl ifanc â phrofiad o ofal wrth y Senedd flaenorol, er enghraifft, fod rhai athrawon ysgol wedi ei gwneud hi'n amlwg iawn eu bod mewn gofal, sy'n golygu na fyddent byth yn cael seibiant o'u profiad o'r system ofal. Fe wnaethant ddweud wrth y Senedd flaenorol mai ychydig iawn o gefnogaeth a gawsant i'w helpu i symud ymlaen o leoliadau maeth ac nad oedd ganddynt y sgiliau sylfaenol sydd eu hangen i fyw'n annibynnol.

Gwyddom fod pobl sy'n gadael gofal wedi eu tangynrychioli mewn prifysgolion ac maent ar yr hyn y mae Crisis yn ei ddisgrifio fel 'llwybr rhagweladwy' i ddigartrefedd. Yn ôl y Gymdeithas Genedlaethol er Atal Creulondeb i Blant, maent oddeutu pedair gwaith yn fwy tebygol o fod ag angen iechyd meddwl o'i gymharu â phlant sy'n byw gyda'u teuluoedd biolegol. Mae gweithwyr proffesiynol ac academyddion wedi dweud yn glir iawn nad yw rhianta corfforaethol wedi bod yn cyflawni ar gyfer plant a phobl ifanc sydd â phrofiad o ofal.

Mae rhieni'n cael cam hefyd. Mae ymchwil yn dangos bod rhieni sy'n mynd trwy achos gofal unwaith yn fwy tebygol o wynebu achos eto gyda phlant dilynol. Cafodd 47 y cant o fabanod newydd-anedig sy'n destunau achos gofal yn Lloegr eu geni i famau a oedd wedi cael plant a oedd yn destunau achos gofal o'r blaen. Canfu Arsyllfa Cyfiawnder Teuluol Nuffield fod mamau a thadau sydd â chysylltiad mynych ag achos gofal yn delio â thrawma cymhleth a heb ei ddatrys, a gaiff ei waethygu gan y profiad yn y llys. Mae'r dadleuon ymosodol, iaith ffurfiol a phroses amhersonol yn gwaethygu pryderon ac yn sbarduno ymddygiadau hunan-amddiffynnol, sy'n effeithio'n negyddol ar y berthynas rhwng yr uned broffesiynol a'r uned deuluol. Mae rhieni'n teimlo na chânt eu clywed. Fel y canfu'r adolygiad annibynnol o ofal cymdeithasol plant yn 2022, mae achosion llys, yn ôl eu natur, yn ymosodol ac mae iddynt gost ddynol ac economaidd uchel.

Aelodau, nid oes raid iddi fod fel hyn. Mae yna ffordd arall: llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol (FDAC). Sut y mae'r rhain yn wahanol? Rwyf am ateb trwy ddyfynnu geiriau rhiant yr oedd eu plant wedi'u cymryd o'u gofal cyn hynny, gan gymharu proses FDAC â'r broses safonol. Am y broses safonol, dywedodd, 'Roeddem yn teimlo nad oedd gennym lais a'n bod ni'n ddi-rym, a'n bod yn cael ein cyhuddo o bethau ac nad oedd cyfle i amddiffyn ein hunain.' Wrth siarad am broses y llys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol, dywedodd yr un rhiant, 'Mae'n teimlo fel pe bai gennym bŵer i ddweud ein dweud, cael pethau wedi'u gwneud, cael ein hochr ni wedi ei chlywed, ac yna maent yn ceisio gweithio gyda ni i wella pethau a chwrdd yn y canol.'

Yn wahanol i achos safonol, mae FDAC yn defnyddio dull sy'n ystyriol o drawma, sy'n cynnwys gwrando ar rieni heb farnu, canolbwyntio ar gryfderau rhieni a'r adnoddau sydd ganddynt ar gael iddynt ar hyn o bryd, a chaniatáu hyblygrwydd. Mae rhieni'n cael gweithiwr allweddol o dîm FDAC a barnwr sy'n rhoi cymorth iddynt a dull datrys problemau. Mae yna brofion camddefnyddio sylweddau wythnosol, sy'n cynnwys y rhieni, ac adolygiadau bob pythefnos gan rai nad ydynt yn gyfreithwyr gyda monitro cyfreithiol cyson sy'n creu fforwm i farnwyr a gweithwyr proffesiynol ddatrys problemau gyda'r rhieni, gosod nodau clir a dirprwyo tasgau ar gyfer y pythefnos nesaf. Mae gan rieni dîm amlddisgyblaethol i'w cefnogi, sy'n eu helpu i gael mynediad at wasanaethau ac asiantaethau. Maent yn darparu gwybodaeth dryloyw ac yn sefydlu sawl sesiwn yr wythnos i fynd i'r afael â'r cynllun ymyrraeth.

Yn amlwg, mae'n fodel gwahanol iawn i'r broses safonol, ond sut y mae cael teuluoedd yno? Un her a gododd o'r treial yng Nghymru oedd bod nifer yr atgyfeiriadau'n cael ei lesteirio gan ddryswch ynghylch y trothwy. Credid bod gweithwyr proffesiynol yn sgrinio atgyfeiriadau eu hunain rhag blaen a dim ond yn atgyfeirio os oedd camddefnydd rhieni o sylweddau'n arbennig o ddifrifol. Roedd rhai cynrychiolwyr cyfreithiol o dan yr argraff mai'r awdurdod lleol oedd yn gyfrifol am benderfynu pa achos oedd yn cyrraedd y trothwy, ac awgrymodd y barnwr fod diffyg ymwybyddiaeth a sylw cyffredinol i'r model.

Gellir goresgyn y diffyg ymwybyddiaeth pan fyddwn yn dilyn y model a ddefnyddir yn Llundain, sef bod y trothwy arferol ar gyfer achos yn berthnasol, sy'n golygu os nad yw teulu'n cael ei ddewis ar gyfer y model, byddant yn wynebu'r llys achosion teulu arferol yn lle hynny, a bydd teulu'n gymwys os oes ganddynt hanes o gamddefnyddio cyffuriau neu alcohol gan rieni. Felly, gan ein bod yn gwybod bellach beth yw'r llysoedd hyn, rwyf am ddangos i chi pam y mae'r llysoedd FDAC yn fodel mwy effeithiol.

Canfu'r gwerthusiad o'r llys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yng Nghymru fod nifer y rhieni sy'n camddefnyddio sylweddau wedi gostwng o 83 y cant ar ddechrau'r broses i 54 y cant. Gostyngodd nifer y rhieni sy'n camddefnyddio alcohol, diolch i'r achosion FDAC, o 91 y cant i 60 y cant. Nid yw'n berffaith, ond mae'n welliant amlwg. Gostyngodd nifer y rhieni a gofnodwyd fel rhai a oedd yn camddefnyddio cyffuriau o 94 y cant i 51 y cant. Canfu'r rhai a gefnogwyd gan brofiad o lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn Lloegr, ac yn fwy diweddar, gwerthusiad o effaith FDAC yn genedlaethol, fod cyfran uwch o rieni wedi rhoi'r gorau i gamddefnyddio cyffuriau neu alcohol erbyn diwedd yr achos FDAC. Dangosodd y cynllun peilot yng Nghymru fod nifer y plant yng ngofal un neu'r ddau riant wedi mwy na dyblu o ddechrau achos FDAC i'w ddiwedd. Caiff hynny ei gefnogi, unwaith eto, gan astudiaeth yn Lloegr, a ganfu fod 52 y cant o blant wedi cael eu dychwelyd at eu rhieni, o'i gymharu â dim ond 13 y cant yn y broses safonol. Fe wnaeth y timau teuluol bron â haneru nifer y plant a gafodd eu rhoi yng ngofal awdurdodau lleol. Dyna fwy o unedau teuluol wedi'u cadw gyda'i gilydd.

Ceir manteision profedig eraill hefyd. Nid yw'n syndod fod yr adborth gan rieni'n hynod gadarnhaol. Gwelodd gwerthusiad tîm swydd Bedford rieni'n disgrifio'r broses fel un anfeirniadol a chynhwysol, tra bod rhieni yn Llundain yn disgrifio'r system fel un drawsnewidiol. Ac yma yng Nghymru, disgrifiodd rhiant a gafodd eu haduno â'u plentyn ar ddiwedd yr achos FDAC y gwasanaeth fel achubwr bywyd a dywedodd, 'Mae fy mywyd yn ôl ar y trywydd iawn oherwydd tîm FDAC. Ni allaf eu hargymell ddigon.' 'Ni allaf eu hargymell ddigon'—am gyferbyniad â'r ffordd y mae rhieni'n teimlo am y broses safonol.

Er bod gan Loegr 13 o'r timau arbenigol hyn, mae'n fethiant difrifol nad oes gennym ni un yng Nghymru. Mae'r sefyllfa bresennol yn mynd yn groes i argymhelliad 35 yr adroddiad 'Cyfiawnder yng Nghymru i Bobl Cymru'. Mae'n mynd yn groes i'r argymhelliad yn y gwerthusiad o'r cynllun peilot Cymreig. Mae'n mynd yn groes i fuddiannau gorau plant, pobl ifanc a'u rhieni. Nid oes unrhyw reswm pam na ellir atal yr anghyfiawnder hwn. Caiff hyn ei gadarnhau wrth ystyried yr achos economaidd hefyd.

Mae dadansoddiad economaidd y Ganolfan Arloesi ym maes Cyfiawnder a Mutual Ventures yn dangos bod £3 yn cael ei gynhyrchu mewn arbedion i'r trethdalwr am bob £1 a werir ar weithrediadau FDAC. Mae'n bwysig iawn ystyried gostyngiad yng nghost gwasanaethau plant, yn enwedig pan ystyriwn fod gorwariant mewn awdurdodau lleol yng Nghymru yn deillio o ofal cymdeithasol plant y llynedd yn unig bron yn £30 miliwn. Gan gofio'r budd i'r trethdalwr, y budd i rai o'n plant mwyaf agored i niwed a'r budd i rai o'n rhieni mwyaf agored i niwed, rwy'n annog y Senedd i gefnogi fy nghynnig heddiw. Gadewch inni greu system ofal gyda'n gilydd sy'n adeiladu, nid yn chwalu teuluoedd. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I was three weeks old when I came into care in Newport. I was seven when I was adopted. So, when the Senedd talks about children whose parents cannot look after them, I am not talking about a policy area, I'm talking about the thing that decided my life before I could speak. That does not make me an expert on anybody else's family, but I think a great deal about the moment before a child is taken into care, because nearly everything we do for children, like me, happens afterwards, when the hardest thing has happened.

In December 2021, Wales opened a court designed for exactly that moment, a family drug and alcohol court sitting in Cardiff, serving families from Cardiff and the Vale, with three judges trained for it. It cost £450,000. In November 2023, it closed, but not because it failed. Researchers at Cardiff University looked at it and found that it worked here, that parents were getting better, that children's lives were changing. They said that Wales should keep it and build on it. The judge who sat in it wrote down his regret in the judgment. He could see what it meant for the families still in front of him. It closed because the money ran out.

Let me tell you about what that court actually did. A judge who heard your case properly, rather than whoever happened to be sitting that day. A team of people around you who were there to help, not to judge. Parents were given a chance to get clean while the case was still running, instead of being watched and measured and found wanting. And when it worked, a child stayed at home. They were not moved, not placed, not separated from their brothers and their sisters—at home with a mother who had been given the help that she so desperately needed. Everywhere else, these cases take about a year. Think about what a year is to a three-year-old. It is a sixth of everything they have ever known spent waiting to be told where they are going to live.

Let's be clear about what I'm not saying. I'm not saying that every family can be saved. Some children are inevitably safer away from their parents, and the courts are right when they say so. I'm one of those children. But care should be the last thing we try, not the first thing that happens. A child who stays safely at home keeps their family, their school and their peer group, their brothers and their sisters. A child who goes into care loses all three, and we become their parent instead.

The Senedd agreed unanimously across four parties that we do take corporate parenting seriously—that when the state steps into a parent's place, it accepts the parental responsibility. I believe that, but a good parent does not wait until a child has already lost their family before deciding to help. If we mean what we said about corporate parenting, it cannot begin at the moment a child comes into care; it has to begin before.

The question is not whether this works. England has many of these teams, but Wales has none. The question is why Wales could not keep it. Wales paid for this court; Wales paid for a court in a justice system it does not control. The courts belong to Westminster—the judges, the rules, the whole structure. But what belong to us are the social workers, the health services, the drug and alcohol teams—the people who made the court work, funded from here.

Wales could pay for a pilot; what Wales could not do was put it on a statutory footing, because that at the moment is not ours to build. Wales could fund the team year after year and still never make the court itself a permanent part of the justice system. When the money ran out, there was nothing underneath it—it wasn't on a statutory footing. So, this is what happened—not a decision anyone took, not a judgment that this was wrong for Wales, just a court that existed on borrowed time and stopped existing.

The Commission on Justice in Wales spent four years looking at this. It said in 2019 that these courts should be established in Wales. It also said that justice and policing should be devolved, because a system split down the middle serves nobody, least of all the people caught in the middle of it. I think they were right, and I do not know of a clearer example than this one. Wales paid for this court. It worked, it closed, and Wales never had the power to make it permanent in law. It was never able to be put on a statutory footing—there's no clearer example than this.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Roeddwn i'n dair wythnos oed pan gefais fy nerbyn i ofal yng Nghasnewydd. Roeddwn i'n saith oed pan gefais fy mabwysiadu. Felly, pan fo'r Senedd yn sôn am blant nad yw eu rhieni'n gallu gofalu amdanynt, nid wyf yn siarad am faes polisi, rwy'n sôn am y peth a benderfynodd lwybr fy mywyd i cyn imi allu siarad. Nid yw hynny'n fy ngwneud i'n arbenigwr ar deulu unrhyw un arall, ond rwy'n meddwl llawer am y foment cyn i blentyn gael ei dderbyn i ofal, oherwydd mae bron bopeth a wnawn i blant fel fi yn digwydd wedyn, pan fo'r peth anoddaf wedi digwydd.

Ym mis Rhagfyr 2021, agorodd Cymru lys a luniwyd ar gyfer yr union foment honno, llys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yng Nghaerdydd, i wasanaethu teuluoedd o Gaerdydd a'r Fro, gyda thri barnwr wedi'u hyfforddi ar ei gyfer. Costiodd £450,000. Ym mis Tachwedd 2023, fe gaeodd, ond nid oherwydd ei fod wedi methu. Edrychodd ymchwilwyr ym Mhrifysgol Caerdydd arno a chanfod ei fod yn gweithio yma, fod rhieni'n gwella, fod bywydau plant yn newid. Fe wnaethant ddweud y dylai Cymru ei gadw ac adeiladu arno. Ysgrifennodd y barnwr a eisteddai ynddo ei fod yn gresynu ynghylch y penderfyniad. Gallai weld beth oedd yn ei olygu i'r teuluoedd a oedd yn dal o'i flaen. Fe gaeodd am fod yr arian wedi dod i ben.

Gadewch imi ddweud wrthych beth oedd y llys hwnnw'n ei wneud mewn gwirionedd. Barnwr a wrandawai'n iawn ar eich achos, yn hytrach na phwy bynnag sy'n digwydd bod yn eistedd y diwrnod hwnnw. Tîm o bobl o'ch cwmpas a oedd yno i helpu, nid i farnu. Rhoddwyd cyfle i rieni roi'r gorau i gamddefnyddio sylweddau tra bod yr achos yn dal ar y gweill, yn hytrach na chael eu gwylio a'u mesur a'u barnu. A phan weithiai, byddai plentyn yn aros gartref. Ni chaent eu symud, ni chaent eu lleoli, ni chaent eu gwahanu oddi wrth eu brodyr a'u chwiorydd—gartref gyda mam a oedd wedi cael yr help yr oedd hi ei angen mor daer. Ym mhob man arall, mae'r achosion hyn yn cymryd tua blwyddyn. Meddyliwch beth yw blwyddyn i blentyn tair oed. Mae'n draean o bopeth y maent erioed wedi'i wybod yn cael ei dreulio'n aros i gael gwybod ble byddant yn byw.

Gadewch inni fod yn glir am yr hyn nad wyf yn ei ddweud. Nid wyf yn dweud y gellir achub pob teulu. Mae rhai plant yn anochel yn fwy diogel allan o ofal eu rhieni, ac mae'r llysoedd yn iawn pan fyddant yn dweud hynny. Rwy'n un o'r plant hynny. Ond dylai gofal fod y peth olaf y ceisiwn ei wneud, nid y peth cyntaf sy'n digwydd. Mae plentyn sy'n aros yn ddiogel gartref yn cadw eu teulu, eu hysgol a'u grŵp cyfoedion, eu brodyr a'u chwiorydd. Mae plentyn sy'n mynd i ofal yn colli'r tri, ac rydym ni'n dod yn rhiant iddynt yn lle hynny.

Cytunodd y Senedd yn unfrydol ar draws pedair plaid ein bod o ddifrif ynghylch rhianta corfforaethol—pan fydd y wladwriaeth yn camu i le rhiant, mae'n derbyn cyfrifoldeb rhiant. Rwy'n credu hynny, ond nid yw rhiant da yn aros nes bod plentyn eisoes wedi colli eu teulu cyn penderfynu helpu. Os ydym yn golygu'r hyn a ddywedasom am rianta corfforaethol, ni all ddechrau y foment y caiff plentyn ei dderbyn i ofal; rhaid iddo ddechrau cyn hynny.

Nid a yw hyn yn gweithio yw'r cwestiwn. Mae gan Loegr lawer o'r timau hyn, ond nid oes un gan Gymru. Y cwestiwn yw pam na allai Cymru ei gadw. Talodd Cymru am y llys hwn; talodd Cymru am lys mewn system gyfiawnder nad yw'n ei rheoli. Mae'r llysoedd yn perthyn i San Steffan—y barnwyr, y rheolau, yr holl strwythur. Ond yr hyn sy'n perthyn i ni yw'r gweithwyr cymdeithasol, y gwasanaethau iechyd, y timau cyffuriau ac alcohol—y bobl a wnaeth i'r llys weithio, wedi'u hariannu o'r fan hon.

Gallai Cymru dalu am gynllun peilot; yr hyn na allai Cymru ei wneud oedd ei roi ar sail statudol, oherwydd nid yw hynny'n rhywbeth y cawn ni ei adeiladu ar hyn o bryd. Gallai Cymru ariannu'r tîm flwyddyn ar ôl blwyddyn a dal i fethu gwneud y llys ei hun yn rhan barhaol o'r system gyfiawnder. Pan ddaeth yr arian i ben, nid oedd unrhyw beth oddi tano—nid oedd ar sail statudol. Felly, dyma beth a ddigwyddodd—nid penderfyniad a gymerwyd gan unrhyw un, nid dyfarniad fod hyn yn anghywir i Gymru, dim ond llys a oedd yn bodoli ar amser benthyg ac a ddaeth i ben.

Treuliodd y Comisiwn ar Gyfiawnder yng Nghymru bedair blynedd yn edrych ar hyn. Dywedodd yn 2019 y dylai'r llysoedd hyn gael eu sefydlu yng Nghymru. Dywedodd hefyd y dylid datganoli cyfiawnder a phlismona, oherwydd nid yw system sydd wedi'i rhannu i lawr y canol yn gwasanaethu neb, llai fyth y bobl sy'n cael eu dal yn y canol. Rwy'n credu eu bod yn iawn, ac nid wyf yn gwybod am enghraifft gliriach na'r un hon. Fe dalodd Cymru am y llys hwn. Roedd yn gweithio, fe gaeodd, ac ni chafodd Cymru bŵer i'w wneud yn barhaol yn y gyfraith. Ni allai byth mo'i roi ar sail statudol—nid oes enghraifft gliriach na hon.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Can I please thank Tom Montgomery for bringing forward this debate today? I'm pleased to be a co-subscriber of this motion.

Family drug and alcohol courts can play a pivotal role in creating better outcomes for children and parents. By taking a different approach to normal courts, with treatment and practical support, they can help parents overcome substance misuse and help keep families, ultimately, together. In my mind, doing all that we can to keep families together, instead of breaking them up, should indeed be the first course of action. Of course, there will undoubtedly be cases where that isn't appropriate or indeed safe, but families should be given every reasonable chance to stick together. Instead of the court simply deciding whether a child should remain or enter care, these specialist courts aim to give the parent a structured opportunity to address the ongoing problems.

And the evidence is really strong. In England, as we've just heard, a major evaluation of 106 families who went through family drug and alcohol courts found that 40 per cent of mothers and 25 per cent of fathers stopped misusing substances. In comparison, only 25 per cent of mothers and 5 per cent of fathers who went through ordinary care proceedings stopped misusing substances. The long-term data is indeed promising. Five years after proceedings ended, the evaluation found that 46 per cent of mothers had stopped misusing substances and that 37 per cent of families who went through family drug and alcohol courts had been reunited or continued living together.

As well as bringing family benefits, it also fits into the Government's preventative health agenda and can deliver savings to the public purse long term. According to the Centre for Justice Innovation, these courts have the potential to save local authorities nearly £10,000 per case in legal costs compared to the standard care proceedings. The Department for Education echoed these findings with their own analysis, concluding that family drug and alcohol courts generate significant savings whilst also achieving significantly better outcomes for children and families.

Countries around the world, including America and Australia, have some sort of family drug and alcohol court system in place, yet sadly, here in Wales, we do not have anything. The previous Labour Welsh Government committed to introducing these courts here in Wales and launched a pilot. The pilot, which was carried out in Cardiff and the Vale, found that parental substance misuse fell from 83 per cent to 54 per cent, and that the number of children living with one or both parents at the end of proceedings was more than double the number at the start.

Last year, the previous Welsh Government established a working group to consider scaling, funding and the wider use of family drug and alcohol courts. Since then, we haven't heard anything. Given that the proposal of introducing family drug and alcohol courts here in Wales appears to have cross-party support, from what I'm hearing and from what I'm seeing, it is now time for this Plaid Cymru Government to pick up this mantle and put this back on the agenda. Thank you.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
A gaf i ddiolch i Tom Montgomery am gyflwyno'r ddadl hon heddiw? Rwy'n falch o'r cyfle i gyd-gyflwyno’r cynnig hwn.

Gall llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol chwarae rhan hollbwysig yn creu canlyniadau gwell i blant a rhieni. Drwy fabwysiadu dull o weithredu gwahanol i lysoedd arferol, gyda thriniaeth a chymorth ymarferol, gallant helpu rhieni i oresgyn problemau camddefnyddio sylweddau a helpu i gadw teuluoedd gyda'i gilydd yn y pen draw. Yn fy marn i, gwneud popeth yn ein gallu i gadw teuluoedd gyda'i gilydd, yn hytrach na'u chwalu, ddylai fod y cam cyntaf. Wrth gwrs, bydd achosion lle nad yw hynny'n briodol, nac yn ddiogel yn wir, ond dylid rhoi pob cyfle rhesymol i deuluoedd aros gyda'i gilydd. Yn hytrach na bod y llys yn penderfynu a ddylai plentyn aros neu fynd i ofal, nod y llysoedd arbenigol hyn yw rhoi cyfle strwythuredig i'r rhiant fynd i'r afael â'r problemau parhaus.

Ac mae'r dystiolaeth yn gryf iawn. Yn Lloegr, fel rydym newydd ei glywed, canfu gwerthusiad mawr o 106 o deuluoedd a aeth drwy lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol fod 40 y cant o famau a 25 y cant o dadau wedi rhoi'r gorau i gamddefnyddio sylweddau. Mewn cymhariaeth, dim ond 25 y cant o famau a 5 y cant o dadau a aeth drwy achosion gofal cyffredin a roddodd y gorau i gamddefnyddio sylweddau. Mae'r data hirdymor yn addawol yn wir. Bum mlynedd ar ôl diwedd eu hachosion, canfu'r gwerthusiad fod 46 y cant o famau wedi rhoi'r gorau i gamddefnyddio sylweddau a bod 37 y cant o deuluoedd a aeth drwy lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol wedi dod yn ôl at ei gilydd neu wedi parhau i fyw gyda'i gilydd.

Yn ogystal â darparu manteision teuluol, mae hefyd yn cyd-fynd ag agenda iechyd ataliol y Llywodraeth a gall arbed arian i bwrs y wlad yn y tymor hir. Yn ôl y Ganolfan Arloesi ym maes Cyfiawnder, mae gan y llysoedd hyn botensial i arbed bron i £10,000 yr achos i awdurdodau lleol mewn costau cyfreithiol o gymharu â’r achosion gofal safonol. Adleisiodd yr Adran Addysg y canfyddiadau hyn gyda’u dadansoddiad eu hunain, gan ddod i’r casgliad fod llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn cynhyrchu arbedion sylweddol gan gyflawni canlyniadau llawer gwell i blant a theuluoedd ar yr un pryd.

Mae gan wledydd ledled y byd, gan gynnwys America ac Awstralia, ryw fath o system llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol ar waith, ond yn anffodus, yma yng Nghymru, nid oes gennym unrhyw beth. Ymrwymodd Llywodraeth Lafur flaenorol Cymru i gyflwyno'r llysoedd hyn yma yng Nghymru a lansiodd gynllun peilot. Canfu'r cynllun peilot, a gynhaliwyd yng Nghaerdydd a'r Fro, fod lefel camddefnyddio sylweddau gan rieni wedi gostwng o 83 y cant i 54 y cant, a bod nifer y plant sy'n byw gydag un neu'r ddau riant ar ddiwedd eu hachos yn fwy na dwbl y nifer ar y dechrau.

Y llynedd, sefydlodd Llywodraeth flaenorol Cymru weithgor i ystyried ehangu, ariannu a gwneud defnydd ehangach o lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol. Ers hynny, nid ydym wedi clywed unrhyw beth. O ystyried bod y cynnig i gyflwyno llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yma yng Nghymru i'w weld yn denu cefnogaeth drawsbleidiol, o'r hyn a glywaf ac o'r hyn a welaf, mae'n bryd i Lywodraeth Plaid Cymru ysgwyddo'r cyfrifoldeb a rhoi hyn yn ôl ar yr agenda. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I speak to support this motion and the powerful case that my colleagues in this Chamber have already established. 

Family drug and alcohol courts were something that I was not very aware of before Tom brought this forward, so I'm really pleased that we're talking about it today. Of course, it was not dreamt up in a think tank; it was born of a judge's frustration. District judge Nicholas Crichton sat in a family court in London and watched the same mothers return again and again. He asked a simple question:

'Just what is it that family courts are there to do? Just take away children?'

'If we are looking to remove the 8th, 9th or 10th child, the family courts can't be doing very well by this family'.

Inspired by family treatment courts in the United States, he set up the first London FDAC in 2008. As we've heard in the Chamber already, an international review of 17 studies of family drug treatment courts found that families were significantly more likely to be reunited. From Australia to New Zealand, this works. 

The most senior family judge in England and Wales, Sir Andrew McFarlane, said:

'The ultimate goal remains for FDAC courts to be available in all areas of England and Wales.'

England and Wales. Members, the judiciary is ready, and it is waiting for us. 

Mothers reunited through FDAC were more than likely to still be off drugs or alcohol five years on. This is not a performance for the courtroom. This is a life rebuilt. Even when children cannot go home, FDAC keeps parents in treatment so that they can still play a healthy part in their children's lives, so the next baby does not end up in court and maybe taken away from the family. 

The motion asks that FDACs form part of a strategy to keep children out of care. Bedfordshire shows the way, and we've heard quotes from Bedfordshire across the Chamber today. Bedfordshire is not just about children's services running this. It is also backed by the local integrated care board, who evaluate its work and bring support from every partner. Here in Wales, we have partners around the table already. We have health boards, we have substance misuse area planning boards, we have regional partnership boards, and we have police and crime commissioners—for now. Every one of them gains when a parent recovers and a family stays together. Every one of those organisations, and us, should help own this. 

I urge Members to support this motion. As Tom said, we need to build a care system in Wales that builds, not breaks, families.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Rwy'n siarad i gefnogi'r cynnig hwn a'r achos cryf y mae fy nghyd-Aelodau eisoes wedi'i sefydlu yn y Siambr hon.

Roedd llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn rhywbeth nad oeddwn yn ymwybodol iawn ohonynt cyn i Tom gyflwyno hyn, felly rwy'n falch iawn ein bod yn siarad amdanynt heddiw. Wrth gwrs, ni chafodd hyn ei lunio mewn melin drafod; mae'n deillio o rwystredigaeth barnwr. Eisteddai'r barnwr rhanbarth Nicholas Crichton mewn llys teulu yn Llundain a gwelodd yr un mamau'n dychwelyd dro ar ôl tro. Gofynnodd gwestiwn syml:

'Beth yn union yw pwrpas llysoedd teulu? Ai dim ond i fynd â phlant oddi ar eu rhieni?'

'Os ydym yn bwriadu mynd â'r 8fed, 9fed neu 10fed plentyn, ni all y llysoedd teulu fod yn gwneud llawer o les i'r teulu hwn'.

Wedi'i ysbrydoli gan lysoedd triniaeth teulu yn yr Unol Daleithiau, sefydlodd y barnwr y llys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol cyntaf yn Llundain yn 2008. Fel rydym eisoes wedi'i glywed yn y Siambr, canfu adolygiad rhyngwladol o 17 astudiaeth o lysoedd triniaeth cyffuriau teuluol fod teuluoedd yn llawer mwy tebygol o gael eu hailuno. O Awstralia i Seland Newydd, mae hyn yn gweithio.

Dywedodd y barnwr teulu uchaf yng Nghymru a Lloegr, Syr Andrew McFarlane:

'Y nod yn y pen draw yw bod llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol ar gael ym mhob ardal o Gymru a Lloegr.'

Cymru a Lloegr. Aelodau, mae'r farnwriaeth yn barod, ac mae'n aros amdanom.

Roedd mamau a adunwyd drwy lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn fwy tebygol o fod oddi ar gyffuriau neu alcohol bum mlynedd yn ddiweddarach. Nid perfformiad ar gyfer y llys yw hwn. Mae hwn yn fywyd wedi'i ailadeiladu. Hyd yn oed pan na all plant fynd adref, mae llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn cadw rhieni mewn triniaeth fel y gallant barhau i chwarae rhan iach ym mywydau eu plant, fel nad yw'r babi nesaf yn mynd i'r llys ac efallai'n cael eu cymryd oddi wrth y teulu.

Mae'r cynnig yn galw am wneud llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn rhan o strategaeth i gadw plant allan o ofal. Mae swydd Bedford yn arwain y ffordd, ac rydym wedi clywed dyfyniadau o swydd Bedford ar draws y Siambr heddiw. Mae swydd Bedford yn sicrhau bod mwy na gwasanaethau plant yn rhedeg hyn. Caiff ei gefnogi hefyd gan y bwrdd gofal integredig lleol, sy'n gwerthuso ei waith ac yn dod â chefnogaeth gan bob partner. Yma yng Nghymru, mae gennym bartneriaid o amgylch y bwrdd yn barod. Mae gennym fyrddau iechyd, mae gennym fyrddau cynllunio ardal camddefnyddio sylweddau, mae gennym fyrddau partneriaeth rhanbarthol, ac mae gennym gomisiynwyr heddlu a throseddu—am nawr. Mae pob un ohonynt yn elwa pan fydd rhiant yn gwella a theulu'n aros gyda'i gilydd. Dylai pob un o'r sefydliadau hynny, a ninnau, helpu i sicrhau hyn.

Rwy'n annog yr Aelodau i gefnogi'r cynnig hwn. Fel y dywedodd Tom, mae angen inni adeiladu system ofal yng Nghymru sy'n adeiladu, nid yn chwalu, teuluoedd.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Thank you very much to Tom for raising this issue. This is actually the Senedd at its best, when we hear views on something really important for our citizens, but, in this case, really important for our children. I've worked in childcare proceedings over 25 years, under both FDAC in London and non-FDAC courts as well. As you've heard, in England, there are 13 teams working in 18 courts. In Wales, we have none. 

Rhys ab Owen and I, in the previous Senedd, raised the need for FDACs. We've done this since 2023. And here we are, three years later, with no FDAC in Wales. So, I'm giving a warning, if I may: we do need to hear a plan for how we're going to get FDAC into Wales. There is no doubt about it that FDACs save money, save lives, and give our children the best chance. 

I want to paint a picture of some of the work that I did as a child protection social worker. We know that the best place for a child is with their parents. But imagine if you were a parent, possibly with a care background, possibly experiencing mental health difficulties, stressed, living in poverty. I've described it as you are trying desperately to get up the escalator that is coming down—you have very little chance. So, you start using drugs and alcohol as a way of forgetting about it and trying to remove yourself from the world you're in. You don't mean to get addicted, but it happens. You have your own children, and you can't look after them. Social services—people like myself—then become involved. As a parent, you fight—of course you do; every single parent wants to keep their child. There is absolutely no doubt, in terms of my 25 years of experience, that that is the case. But you have no resources. You have no services that work with you. Instead, services make you jump through hoops. More stress, more drugs, more alcohol.

That's what happens in normal family court proceedings. You do not have the services there ready for you. They are there to try and make you show that you want to keep your child, and that stresses you out even more. Or you go to FDAC, and you have a chance, and, most importantly, your children have a chance. They have the best chance that they can have in life to stay with you.

I'll finish by saying the evidence is there. It's indisputable. Family judges that I've worked with—because I did work in the London principal registry—have said it very clearly. I don't know what else the Welsh Government needs to hear. But you need to hear the evidence and you need to act on it, because children cannot wait any longer. Please, just do it. Diolch yn fawr iawn.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch yn fawr iawn i Tom am godi'r mater hwn. Dyma'r Senedd ar ei gorau, pan fyddwn yn clywed safbwyntiau ar rywbeth sy'n wirioneddol bwysig i'n dinasyddion, ond yn yr achos hwn, yn wirioneddol bwysig i'n plant. Rwyf wedi gweithio mewn achosion gofal plant am dros 25 mlynedd, o dan lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn Llundain a llysoedd nad ydynt yn llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol hefyd. Fel y clywsoch, yn Lloegr, mae 13 tîm yn gweithio mewn 18 llys. Yng Nghymru, nid oes gennym un.

Fe wnaeth Rhys ab Owen a minnau, yn y Senedd flaenorol, godi'r angen am lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol. Rydym wedi gwneud hyn ers 2023. A dyma ni, dair blynedd yn ddiweddarach, heb lys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yng Nghymru. Felly, rwy'n rhoi rhybudd, os caf: mae angen inni glywed cynllun ar gyfer sut rydym yn mynd i gael llys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yng Nghymru. Nid oes amheuaeth fod llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn arbed arian, yn achub bywydau, ac yn rhoi'r cyfle gorau i'n plant.

Hoffwn baentio darlun o rywfaint o'r gwaith a wneuthum fel gweithiwr cymdeithasol amddiffyn plant. Gwyddom mai'r lle gorau i blentyn yw gyda'u rhieni. Ond dychmygwch pe baech yn rhiant, â chefndir gofal o bosibl, o bosibl yn wynebu anawsterau iechyd meddwl, o dan straen, yn byw mewn tlodi. Rwyf wedi'i ddisgrifio fel pe baech chi'n ymdrechu'n daer i ddringo grisiau symudol sy'n dod i lawr—nid oes gennych fawr o obaith. Felly, rydych chi'n dechrau defnyddio cyffuriau ac alcohol fel ffordd o anghofio am y peth a cheisio tynnu eich hun allan o'r byd rydych chi ynddo. Nid ydych yn bwriadu mynd yn gaeth, ond mae'n digwydd. Mae gennych eich plant eich hun, ac ni allwch ofalu amdanynt. Yna mae gwasanaethau cymdeithasol—pobl fel fi—yn dod yn rhan o bethau. Fel rhiant, rydych chi'n ymladd—wrth gwrs eich bod; mae pob rhiant eisiau cadw eu plentyn. Nid oes unrhyw amheuaeth o gwbl ynglŷn â hynny, yn fy 25 mlynedd o brofiad. Ond nid oes gennych unrhyw adnoddau. Nid oes gennych unrhyw wasanaethau sy'n gweithio gyda chi. Yn hytrach, mae gwasanaethau'n eich rhoi drwy'r felin. Mwy o straen, mwy o gyffuriau, mwy o alcohol.

Dyna sy'n digwydd mewn achosion llys teulu arferol. Nid oes gennych y gwasanaethau yno yn barod i chi. Maent yno i geisio gwneud ichi ddangos eich bod eisiau cadw eich plentyn, ac mae hynny'n eich rhoi dan fwy fyth o straen. Neu rydych chi'n mynd i lys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol, ac mae gennych gyfle, ac yn bwysicaf oll, mae gan eich plant gyfle. Mae ganddynt y cyfle gorau y gallant ei gael mewn bywyd i aros gyda chi.

Rwyf am gloi drwy ddweud bod y dystiolaeth yno. Mae'n ddiymwad. Mae barnwyr teulu y gweithiais gyda nhw—gan fy mod yn arfer gweithio ym mhrif gofrestrfa Llundain—wedi dweud hyn yn glir iawn. Nid wyf yn gwybod beth arall sydd angen i Lywodraeth Cymru ei glywed. Ond mae angen ichi glywed y dystiolaeth ac mae angen ichi weithredu arni, gan na all plant aros yn hwy. Os gwelwch yn dda, gwnewch hynny. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I rise today in support of this motion, because, at its heart, this debate is about one thing and one thing only: children. Quite rightly, we have heard a great deal about court processes, social services, addiction, public spending. But behind every statistic is a child whose future may be shaped by the decisions we make in this Chamber today. When a child enters care, it's often because adults around them are struggling with complex problems: substance misuse, poor mental health, trauma, domestic instability. None of those challenges should ever be minimised. But neither should we forget that, wherever it is safe and possible, most children want the same thing: they want love, they want stability, and they want the chance to remain connected to their family.

The reality is that children who enter care often face significant disadvantages later in life. We know care-experienced young people are less likely to attend university, to attain the qualification level that they could have, and are more likely to experience homelessness, and even more likely to experience mental health difficulties as they grow up. Those outcomes are not inevitable, but they are deeply concerning and should compel all of us to ask a simple question: is there a better way of helping families overcome the issues that bring them into the court system in the first place, and if there is, why would we not pursue it?

What strikes me about family drug and alcohol courts is that they do not lower the standards or compromise children's safety; they do the exact opposite. They recognise the best way to protect children, and it's often to address the root causes that place families in crisis and not simply manage the consequences. The evidence presented today shows that, when parents receive intensive support to overcome addiction and address traumas, and child benefit too, more parents successfully stop misusing drugs and alcohol, more families achieve stability, and more children are able to remain safely or return safely to their parents and family. That matters, because every child who can safely remain within a loving family environment is given something that no institution or service can ever truly replace—a sense of belonging, a sense of identity, a sense of permanence.

The Welsh pilot demonstrated that the proportion of children in the care of one or both of their parents more than doubled during FDAC proceedings. Evidence from England shows substantially more children being united with their families compared to conventional proceedings. Those outcomes are not just policy successes, they are life-changing opportunities for children. Children who may stay in the same school, maintain friendships, remain connected to brothers and sisters, preserve relationships with grandparents and wider family networks, and avoid the additional trauma that can accompany family separation.

Of course, there will always be cases where children cannot safely remain at home. In those circumstances, protecting the child must remain our overriding priority. But where recovery is achievable, where parents are willing to engage, and where evidence demonstrates better outcomes, we should ensure those opportunities exist.

What concerns me is that Wales once had a pilot programme, yet today we have nothing—no family drug and alcohol court operating in our nation at all. Meanwhile, England has continued on the journey and expanded the model. That leaves Welsh children with fewer opportunities to benefit from an approach that has repeatedly shown promise. We often speak in this Chamber about early intervention, about prevention, about breaking cycles that pass from one generation to the next. Family drug and alcohol courts embody those principles more perfectly than anything I've ever seen. They are not simply about responding to addiction, they're about giving children the best possible chance of a stable future, they're about preventing trauma rather than merely dealing with the consequence itself, and they are about recognising that helping a parent recover can transform a child's entire life trajectory.

Members, every child deserves safety, every child deserves stability and every child deserves the opportunity to grow up in a nurturing family environment where that can be achieved safely. That is why I support this motion, and that is why I urge my colleagues across the Chamber to support the expansion of family drug and alcohol courts in Wales. Diolch.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Rwy'n codi heddiw i gefnogi'r cynnig hwn, oherwydd yn y bôn, mae a wnelo'r ddadl hon ag un peth ac un peth yn unig: plant. Rydym wedi clywed llawer, a hynny'n gwbl briodol, am brosesau llys, gwasanaethau cymdeithasol, caethiwed, gwariant cyhoeddus. Ond y tu ôl i bob ystadegyn, mae plentyn y gall eu dyfodol gael ei siapio gan y penderfyniadau a wnawn yn y Siambr hon heddiw. Pan fydd plentyn yn mynd i ofal, mae hynny'n aml yn digwydd am fod yr oedolion o'u cwmpas yn ymrafael â phroblemau cymhleth: camddefnyddio sylweddau, iechyd meddwl gwael, trawma, ansefydlogrwydd domestig. Ni ddylid bychanu unrhyw un o'r heriau hynny. Ond ni ddylem anghofio chwaith, lle bynnag y bo'n ddiogel ac yn bosibl, fod y rhan fwyaf o blant eisiau'r un peth: maent eisiau cariad, maent eisiau sefydlogrwydd, ac maent eisiau cyfle i aros yn gysylltiedig â'u teulu.

Y gwir amdani yw bod plant sy'n mynd i ofal yn aml yn wynebu anfanteision sylweddol yn nes ymlaen mewn bywyd. Gwyddom fod pobl ifanc sydd wedi cael profiad o ofal yn llai tebygol o fynychu prifysgol, o ennill cymhwyster ar y lefel y gallent fod wedi'i chyrraedd, ac yn fwy tebygol o brofi digartrefedd, a hyd yn oed yn fwy tebygol o brofi anawsterau iechyd meddwl wrth iddynt dyfu i fyny. Nid yw'r canlyniadau hynny'n anochel, ond maent yn peri cryn bryder, a dylent orfodi pob un ohonom i ofyn cwestiwn syml: a oes ffordd well o helpu teuluoedd i oresgyn y problemau sy'n dod â nhw i mewn i'r system llysoedd yn y lle cyntaf, ac os oes, pam na fyddem yn mynd ar ei thrywydd?

Yr hyn sy'n fy nharo am lysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yw nad ydynt yn gostwng y safonau nac yn peryglu diogelwch plant; maent yn gwneud y gwrthwyneb yn llwyr. Maent yn cydnabod y ffordd orau o amddiffyn plant, ac yn aml, mae a wnelo hynny â mynd i'r afael â'r achosion sylfaenol sy'n rhoi teuluoedd mewn argyfwng yn hytrach na delio â'r canlyniadau yn unig. Mae'r dystiolaeth a gyflwynir heddiw yn dangos, pan fydd rhieni'n cael cymorth dwys i oresgyn caethiwed a delio â thrawma, a budd-dal plant hefyd, fod mwy o rieni'n llwyddo i roi'r gorau i gamddefnyddio cyffuriau ac alcohol, fod mwy o deuluoedd yn cael sefydlogrwydd, a bod mwy o blant yn gallu aros yn ddiogel neu ddychwelyd yn ddiogel at eu rhieni a'u teulu. Mae hynny'n bwysig, gan fod pob plentyn sy'n gallu aros yn ddiogel mewn amgylchedd teuluol cariadus yn cael rhywbeth na all unrhyw sefydliad na gwasanaeth byth gymryd ei le'n iawn—ymdeimlad o berthyn, ymdeimlad o hunaniaeth, ymdeimlad o sefydlogrwydd.

Dangosodd y cynllun peilot yng Nghymru fod cyfran y plant sydd yng ngofal un neu'r ddau riant wedi mwy na dyblu yn ystod achosion llys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol. Mae tystiolaeth o Loegr yn dangos bod llawer mwy o blant yn cael eu huno â'u teuluoedd o gymharu ag achosion llys confensiynol. Nid llwyddiannau polisi yn unig yw'r canlyniadau hynny, maent yn gyfleoedd sy'n newid bywydau plant. Plant a allai aros yn yr un ysgol, cadw ffrindiau, cadw'r cysylltiad â brodyr a chwiorydd, cadw perthynas â neiniau a theidiau a rhwydweithiau teuluol ehangach, ac osgoi'r trawma ychwanegol a all fynd law yn llaw â chael eu gwahanu oddi wrth eu teulu.

Wrth gwrs, bydd yna achosion bob amser lle na all plant aros gartref yn ddiogel. Yn yr amgylchiadau hynny, rhaid i ddiogelu'r plentyn barhau i fod yn brif flaenoriaeth i ni. Ond lle mae adferiad yn bosibl, lle mae rhieni'n barod i ymgysylltu, a lle mae tystiolaeth yn dangos canlyniadau gwell, dylem sicrhau bod y cyfleoedd hynny'n bodoli.

Yr hyn sy'n peri pryder i mi yw bod Cymru wedi cynnal rhaglen beilot ar hyn yn barod, ond heddiw, nid oes gennym unrhyw beth—dim llys teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn gweithredu yn ein gwlad o gwbl. Yn y cyfamser, mae Lloegr wedi parhau ar y daith ac wedi ehangu'r model. Mae hynny'n golygu bod llai o gyfleoedd i blant Cymru elwa o ddull sydd wedi dangos addewid dro ar ôl tro. Rydym yn aml yn siarad yn y Siambr hon am ymyrryd yn gynnar, am atal, am dorri cylchoedd sy'n cael eu hetifeddu o genhedlaeth i genhedlaeth. Mae llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn ymgorffori'r egwyddorion hynny'n fwy perffaith nag unrhyw beth a welais erioed. Nid ymateb i gaethiwed yn unig a wnânt, maent yn rhoi'r cyfle gorau posibl i blant gael dyfodol sefydlog, maent yn atal trawma yn hytrach na delio â'r canlyniad yn unig, ac maent yn cydnabod y gall helpu rhiant i ymadfer drawsnewid llwybr bywyd cyfan plentyn.

Aelodau, mae pob plentyn yn haeddu diogelwch, mae pob plentyn yn haeddu sefydlogrwydd ac mae pob plentyn yn haeddu cyfle i dyfu i fyny mewn amgylchedd teuluol meithringar lle gellir cyflawni hynny'n ddiogel. Dyna pam fy mod yn cefnogi'r cynnig hwn, a dyna pam fy mod yn annog fy nghyd-Aelodau ar draws y Siambr i gefnogi ehangu llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yng Nghymru. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Member_job_title_Welsh: Y Dirprwy Weinidog Gofal Cymdeithasol, Iechyd Meddwl ac Iechyd Menywod
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. A diolch i Tom am ddod â'r ddadl yma gerbron y Senedd, a diolch i'r Aelodau sydd wedi cymryd rhan yn y ddadl eithriadol o bwysig yma. Fel pobl eraill, fe wnes i ddilyn datblygiad y cynllun peilot a chael fy hun yn gofyn cwestiynau tebyg i rai o'r cwestiynau sydd wedi cael eu codi heddiw.

Mae'r dystiolaeth i gefnogi'r model yn gryf. Daeth gwerthusiad y cynllun peilot i'r casgliad y dylid ehangu'r ddarpariaeth yng Nghymru, fel rydyn ni wedi clywed. Mae'r profiad o'r llysoedd hyn yn Lloegr yn dangos canlyniadau cadarnhaol tu hwnt. Fe wnaeth comisiwn Thomas hefyd argymell y dylai dulliau datrys problemau gael eu defnyddio fel mater o drefn, ac y dylai llysoedd o'r fath gael eu sefydlu yng Nghymru.

Wrth gwrs, roedd y gwerthusiad hefyd yn nodi bod sawl rhwystr a chymhlethdod yn perthyn i fodel y llysoedd. Mae hynny yn arbennig o wir yng Nghymru oherwydd y cyfuniad o gyfrifoldebau wedi eu datganoli a heb eu datganoli. Fe wnaeth y comisiwn argymell y dylai'r gyfraith sydd yn ymwneud â phlant a chyfiawnder teuluol yng Nghymru gael ei dwyn ynghyd mewn un system gyfreithiol gydlynol sy'n cyd-fynd â swyddogaethau ym maes iechyd, addysg a lles.

Byddai datganoli cyfiawnder yn creu cyfleoedd i gynllunio gwasanaethau o amgylch anghenion Cymru, yn hytrach na dim ond atgynhyrchu trefniadau sydd wedi'u datblygu mewn mannau eraill. Mae'r profiad gyda'r llysoedd hyn yn dangos mai dim ond un ystyriaeth yw effeithiolrwydd, mae'n rhaid hefyd pwyso a mesur cynaliadwyedd, gofynion y gweithlu a chostau cyfle wrth benderfynu ar y ffordd fwyaf priodol o ddefnyddio adnoddau.

Felly, nid yw hyn yn syml, ond mae gwaith yn mynd yn ei flaen yn y cyd-destun yma. Mae'r model yn gofyn am ymrwymiad gan awdurdodau lleol, y farnwriaeth a'r llysoedd. Mae'n gofyn hefyd am flaenoriaeth gan lawer o wasanaethau, gan gynnwys camddefnyddio sylweddau, cam-drin domestig ac iechyd meddwl.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. And thanks to Tom for bringing this debate before the Senedd, and thank you to Members who have taken part in this vital debate. As others, I followed the development of the pilot scheme and found myself asking similar questions to those that have been raised today.

The evidence to support the model is strong. The evaluation of the pilot scheme concluded that provision in Wales should be expanded, as we've heard. The experience of these courts in England demonstrates positive results. The Thomas commission also recommended that problem-solving approaches should be used routinely, and that such courts should be established in Wales.

Of course, the evaluation also noted that there were many barriers and complications associated with the courts model. That is particularly true in Wales due to the combination of devolved and non-devolved responsibilities. The commission also recommended that the law relating to children and family justice in Wales should be brought together under one coherent legal system that is compatible with functions in the areas of health, education and welfare.

The devolution of justice would create opportunities to plan services around the needs of Wales, rather than just reproducing arrangements that have been developed elsewhere. The experience with these courts demonstrates that effectiveness is only one consideration, we must also weigh up sustainability, workforce requirements and opportunity costs when making decisions on the most appropriate way of using resources.

So, this is not simple, but work is proceeding in this context. The model requires commitment from local authorities, the judiciary and the courts. It also requires prioritisation from many services, including substance misuse, domestic abuse and mental health.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 6. Dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv): Llysoedd Teulu Cyffuriau ac Alcohol
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Family Drug and Alcohol Courts
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
We need to ensure, of course, that funding is available and is sustainable for whatever model we use, because in England the loss of funding has sadly seen some teams disband. This isn't exclusively a decision for the Welsh Government, but we are forefront in relevant conversations in Wales and in the development of the family justice strategy with the Ministry of Justice. Our priority is moving the whole family justice system to a more empathetic and understanding environment, where families feel supported and, crucially, that they have hope. Now, that requires a cultural and systemic change that is wider than just FDACs, of course, and that's already under way. There is so much more that can be done. Last year, the FDAC working group recommended work continues on problem-solving approaches and intensive support for families going through court proceedings.

Dirprwy Lywydd, this is an evolving picture. It was discussed in more depth at regional workshops that were facilitated by the Centre for Justice Innovation earlier this year. The subsequent CJI report highlighted all three regions had a clear appetite for further exploration and development of FDAC problem-solving, trauma-informed approaches within public law proceedings in Wales. The report went on to recognise regional variation, system pressures and the need to build on existing good practice. Overall, the workshops identified a shared set of recommendations to guide the next steps, which will move forward under oversight of the family justice network.

Recently, I met the Deputy First Minister and the Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution, who share policy interests in family justice. We intend to work closely together on reforms to the family justice system, some of which will closely align with those of colleagues in the UK Government, of course, through the family justice strategy.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Mae angen inni sicrhau, wrth gwrs, fod cyllid ar gael a'i fod yn gynaliadwy ar gyfer unrhyw fodel a ddefnyddiwn, oherwydd yn Lloegr, yn anffodus, mae colli cyllid wedi arwain at rai timau'n chwalu. Nid penderfyniad i Lywodraeth Cymru yn unig yw hwn, ond rydym yn chwarae rhan hollbwysig mewn sgyrsiau perthnasol yng Nghymru ac wrth ddatblygu'r strategaeth cyfiawnder teuluol gyda'r Weinyddiaeth Gyfiawnder. Ein blaenoriaeth yw symud y system cyfiawnder teuluol gyfan i amgylchedd mwy empathetig a chydymdeimladol, lle mae teuluoedd yn teimlo eu bod yn cael eu cefnogi, ac yn hollbwysig, fod ganddynt obaith. Nawr, mae hynny'n galw am newid diwylliannol a systemig sy'n ehangach na llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol yn unig wrth gwrs, ac mae hynny eisoes ar y gweill. Mae cymaint mwy y gellir ei wneud. Y llynedd, argymhellodd y gweithgor llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol y dylai gwaith barhau ar ddulliau datrys problemau a chymorth dwys i deuluoedd sy'n mynd drwy achosion llys.

Ddirprwy Lywydd, mae hwn yn ddarlun sy'n esblygu. Fe'i trafodwyd mewn mwy o fanylder mewn gweithdai rhanbarthol a hwyluswyd gan y Ganolfan Arloesi ym maes Cyfiawnder yn gynharach eleni. Tynnodd adroddiad dilynol y ganolfan sylw at yr awydd clir gan y tri rhanbarth i archwilio ymhellach a datblygu dulliau datrys problemau ac ystyriol o drawma'r llysoedd teulu cyffuriau ac alcohol mewn achosion cyfraith gyhoeddus yng Nghymru. Aeth yr adroddiad ymlaen i gydnabod amrywiadau rhanbarthol, pwysau yn y system a'r angen i adeiladu ar arferion da presennol. At ei gilydd, nododd y gweithdai set gyffredin o argymhellion i arwain y camau nesaf, a fydd yn symud ymlaen o dan oruchwyliaeth y rhwydwaith cyfiawnder teuluol.

Yn ddiweddar, cyfarfûm â'r Dirprwy Brif Weinidog a'r Gweinidog dros Effeithiolrwydd Llywodraeth a’r Cyfansoddiad, sy'n rhannu diddordebau polisi mewn cyfiawnder teuluol. Rydym yn bwriadu cydweithio'n agos ar ddiwygiadau i'r system cyfiawnder teuluol, a bydd rhai ohonynt yn cyd-fynd yn agos â rhai swyddogion cyfatebol yn Llywodraeth y DU wrth gwrs, drwy'r strategaeth cyfiawnder teuluol.

I regret the second part of that contribution. Look, I understand, of course, none of us want to cause harm to children, and we have to make sure that the decision that is made takes into account all of these different complexities. If I could be in a position today and say, 'Yes, we are able to do this', of course I would want to do that. I do acknowledge that there is really positive evidence around FDACs.

The options that we need to consider within the Welsh context, which is what the working group have been looking at, need to look at additional structures and whether they would be the best option, looking as well at some of the approaches that have been taken in Scotland, that do follow different but maybe comparable models, and looking to see whether that would be possible. Of course, we need to make sure that whatever future approach that's taken complements existing provision, rather than adding any further complexity. We need to look at sustainability, workforce capacity. We're not delaying for delay's sake. It's so that we make sure that we get this right, although I do utterly appreciate the fervour that is in this Chamber about wanting to move quickly. I understand that entirely.
