XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 7. Reform UK Debate: Regional rugby
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Dwi wedi clywed nifer ohonoch chi'n dweud nad ydych chi eisiau i mi fod yn gyfrifol am bigo'r tîm, a dwi'n falch nad yw'r cyfrifoldeb hwnnw gen i. Yn sicr, dwi ddim yn arbenigwraig. Ond does gen i ddim ychwaith y grym i gyfarwyddo. Mae Undeb Rygbi Cymru yn gorff llywodraethu annibynnol sy'n atebol drwy ei drefniadau cyfansoddiadol ei hun, ac Undeb Rygbi Cymru sy'n gyfrifol am weinyddu rygbi yng Nghymru. Mae ei annibyniaeth hefyd yn cael ei gydnabod o fewn y fframwaith rhyngwladol a sefydlwyd gan World Rugby. Mae'r annibyniaeth hon yn bwysig, ac mae'n bwysig i'w chydnabod. Byddai cyfarwyddyd gwleidyddol dros benderfyniadau yn ymwneud â chwaraeon yn codi cwestiynau cyfreithiol a llywodraethiant difrifol, ac yn bygwth tanseilio'r annibyniaeth y mae chwaraeon rhyngwladol yn dibynnu arni. 

Mae'r ymrwymiad a geisir gan y cynnig hwn, felly, yn un na all Llywodraeth Cymru ei sicrhau. Dyna pam, felly, o ran y gwelliant, rydw i wedi cyfleu'r farn y dylai unrhyw newid sylweddol fel hyn gael ei gefnogi gan achos clir, hirdymor, yn hytrach nag ymateb tymor byr i'r heriau presennol. Rydym yn disgwyl i Undeb Rygbi Cymru egluro sut y byddai unrhyw newid yn cefnogi dyfodol y gêm yng Nghymru, a sut y byddai cynnydd yn cael ei fesur hefyd.

Mae'n rhaid i'r undeb ymgysylltu'n ystyrlon â'r rhai y mae eu cynlluniau arfaethedig yn effeithio arnyn nhw, gan ymgynghori'n llawn ac esbonio'r dystiolaeth y tu ôl i'w cynlluniau, a bod yn glir ynghylch sut y bydd y risgiau'n cael eu rheoli. Mae cefnogwyr a chymunedau yn haeddu mwy na sicrwydd drwy eiriau yn unig. Mi ydych yn iawn—mae nifer ohonoch chi wedi sôn bod angen tryloywder am yr opsiynau sydd dan ystyriaeth, ein bod ni angen gwybod y sail ar gyfer unrhyw benderfyniadau a sut y bydd dyfodol hirdymor y gêm broffesiynol a chymunedol yn cael ei ddiogelu.

Fel dwi wedi'i ddweud a'i rannu yn y sesiwn gwestiynau flaenorol, mi wnes i gyfarfod â'r undeb ym mis Awst, a defnyddio'r cyfle hwnnw i gyfleu'n uniongyrchol iddynt rai o'r pryderon a godwyd gyda mi drwy ohebiaeth. Yn ychwanegol at hynny, yn dilyn trafodaethau yn y pwyllgor diwylliant a chwaraeon, yr holl gwestiynau a godwyd yn y Siambr hon fis diwethaf, a'r ystod o ohebiaeth sydd wedi fy nghyrraedd gan Aelodau o'r Senedd ar ran eich etholwyr, mi wnes i ysgrifennu at yr undeb yn gofyn am ragor o wybodaeth am eu hymgysylltiad â chefnogwyr a chymunedau, am y dystiolaeth sy'n llywio eu dull gweithredu, a sut y bydd yr undeb yn asesu a chyfathrebu goblygiadau penderfyniadau sy'n effeithio ar y gêm ranbarthol. Dwi dal yn disgwyl ymateb i'r llythyr hwnnw, ac, wrth gwrs, mi fyddaf yn diweddaru'r Senedd unwaith rwyf wedi derbyn unrhyw wybodaeth bellach.

Mae angen i ni fod yn glir, felly, nad rôl Llywodraeth Cymru ydy rhedeg rygbi Cymru o ddydd i ddydd, ond dwi eisiau rhoi'r sicrwydd hwn: dydy hyn ddim yn golygu nad ydyn ni'n barod i godi llais, herio a chraffu. Mi fyddwn ni'n parhau i gefnogi cyfranogiad, buddsoddi mewn cyfleusterau a gweithio gyda phartneriaid i gryfhau'r gêm ar bob lefel. O ran y ffigur a nodwyd gan rai, o ran y £434,945 yn 2025-26 a ddarparwyd gan Chwaraeon Cymru, mi oedd hyn, i fod yn glir, i gefnogi datblygiad y gêm ar lawr gwlad. I ni roi hyn mewn cyd-destun, mae hyn yn cynrychioli 0.4 y cant o gyfanswm trosiant Undeb Rygbi Cymru, felly o ran datblygiad y gêm ar lawr gwlad oedd hwnnw.

Mae yna sôn hefyd wedi'i wneud ynglŷn â buddsoddiad a wnaed yn ystod COVID. Mi oedd hynny ynglŷn â grant drwy'r gronfa diogelu chwaraeon gwylwyr. Mi gyfeiriwyd hefyd at y benthyciad masnachol o £18 miliwn a gafodd ei ad-dalu'n llawn yn 2025. Felly, dydy Llywodraeth Cymru na Chwaraeon Cymru ddim yn darparu cyllid ar gyfer y gêm broffesiynol.

Heddiw, mi ydych chi, fel Aelodau, wedi mynegi ar draws y Siambr hon eich pryderon ac wedi cynnig datrysiadau amrywiol, ond yr un peth dwi'n meddwl sydd yn glir rhyngom ni oll ydy bod yna dir cyffredin a'n bod ni eisiau gweld dyfodol llewyrchus i'r gêm yma yng Nghymru, a'n bod ni'n cydnabod y pryderon gwirioneddol sydd yna. Mae hynny'n gofyn am arweinyddiaeth, ymddiriedaeth a gweledigaeth glir gan yr undeb. Mae'n rhaid iddyn nhw drin cefnogwyr fel partneriaid yn y sgwrs honno, nid dim ond eu hysbysu ar ôl i benderfyniadau gael eu gwneud. 

Mae teyrngarwch cefnogwyr wedi cynnal y gêm drwy'r amseroedd da a'r cyfnodau anodd, a dylai eu lleisiau nhw fod yn ganolog i helpu i lunio ei dyfodol. Felly, tra ein bod ni'n cydymdeimlo ag ysbryd y cynnig, ni allwn gefnogi cynnig sy'n gofyn i Lywodraeth Cymru warantu canlyniad nad oes ganddi awdurdod cyfreithlon i'w orfodi. Ond nid yw gwrthod y cynnig hwnnw yr un peth â pheidio â chydnabod y pryderon y tu ôl iddo; mae'r pryderon hynny'n real, maen nhw'n haeddu cael eu clywed ac mae'n hollbwysig i'r undeb eu hateb. Am y rhesymau hynny, gofynnaf i'r Aelodau wrthod y cynnig ond cefnogi gwelliannau Llywodraeth Cymru, fel ein bod yn uno yn ein galwadau ar Undeb Rygbi Cymru i ymgynghori'n drylwyr ac yn dryloyw, a gan gymryd lleisiau'r cefnogwyr, y clybiau a'r cymunedau i ystyriaeth wrth iddyn nhw lunio dyfodol y gêm yma yng Nghymru.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
I've heard many of you saying that you don't want me to be responsible for picking the team, and I'm glad that I don't have that responsibility. I'm not an expert, nor do I have the power to direct. The WRU is an independent governing body accountable through its own constitutional arrangements, and the WRU is responsible for the administration of rugby in Wales. Its independence is also recognised within the international framework established by World Rugby. That independence is important and it's important to recognise it. Issuing political directives on sporting decisions would raise serious legal and governance questions, and would threaten to undermine the independence on which international support depends.

The commitment sought by this motion is, therefore, one that the Welsh Government cannot provide. That's why, turning to the amendment, I've expressed a view that any significant change like this should be supported by a clear, long-term case, rather than a short-term response to the current challenges. We expect the WRU to explain how any change would support the future of the game in Wales and how progress would be measured.

The union must engage meaningfully with those whom the proposed plans will affect by conducting a full consultation and by explaining the evidence underpinning their plans, and they must be clear about how risks will be managed. Supporters and communities deserve more than warm words alone. You're right—many of you have mentioned that there is a need for transparency about the options under consideration and that we need to know the basis for any decisions, and how the long-term future of the professional and community game will be safeguarded.

As I've mentioned and shared in a previous session of questions, I met with the union in August and used that opportunity to convey directly to them some of the concerns raised with me through correspondence. In addition to that, following discussions in the culture and sport committee, and in the questions raised in this Chamber last month, and the range of correspondence that has reached me from Senedd Members on behalf of their constituents, I wrote to the union seeking more information about their engagement with supporters and communities, about the evidence guiding their approach, and how the union will assess and communicate the implications of decisions that are affecting the regional game. I'm still expecting a response to that letter, and, of course, I will update the Senedd once I've received any further information.

We need to be clear, therefore, that it's not the Welsh Government's role to run Welsh rugby from day to day, but I also want to give the assurance that this doesn't mean that we're not willing to scrutinise. We will continue to support participation, invest in facilities and work with partners to strengthen the game at every level. On the figure that was identified by some, in terms of £434,945 in 2025-26, which was provided by Sport Wales, this was, to be clear, to support the development of the game at grass-roots level. To put this in context, this represents 0.4 per cent of the total turnover of the WRU. So, that was for the development of the game at grass-roots level.

There's also been mention made of investment during COVID, and that was about a grant through the spectator sports survival fund. Reference was also made to the commercial loan of £18 million, which was fully repaid in 2025. So, the Welsh Government and Sport Wales do not provide funding for the professional game.

Today, as Members, you have expressed across the Chamber your concerns and you've offered a variety of solutions, but the one thing that is very clear between us all is that we have common ground, that we want to see a prosperous future for the game here in Wales and that we do recognise the genuine concerns that exist. That requires leadership, trust and a clear vision by the union. They have to treat supporters as partners in that conversation, not just informing them after a decision is made.

The loyalty of supporters has sustained the game through good and bad periods, and those voices should be central to shaping the future. So, while we sympathise with the spirit of the motion, we can't support a motion that asks the Welsh Government to guarantee an outcome that it doesn't have legal authority to enforce. But rejecting that motion is not the same thing as not recognising the concerns behind it; those concerns are real and they deserve to be heard, and it's vital for the union to respond to them. For those reasons, I ask Members to reject the motion but to support the Welsh Government amendments, so that we are united in our calls on the Welsh Rugby Union to consult transparently and to consider the voices of communities, clubs and supporters in shaping the future of the game in Wales.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Diolch, Deputy Llywydd. I want to thank all Members who've contributed to what is an important debate. As Members have said in this Chamber, rugby is a lot more. I know that the Minister, in her response, said that she doesn't want to dictate sport, but the Welsh Government, in the past, has stepped in when employment is at risk. As well as clubs that are supported, these regions are employers. Right now for the Welsh economy, the four regions are estimated to contribute between £50 million and £55 million. That is a lot of money. When you say in your motion today that we need to speak with the WRU and give them more time and the rest of it, I think time is running out, Minister. December is coming quickly, and those employees need assurances about whether they'll have a job in the future. So, I'm unafraid today to vote for our motion that's trying to get clarity for people's livelihoods, and I'll never apologise for that. I think the Government has got a role to step in and get involved—
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Hoffwn ddiolch i'r holl Aelodau sydd wedi cyfrannu at y ddadl bwysig hon. Fel y dywedodd yr Aelodau yn y Siambr hon, mae rygbi'n llawer mwy. Rwy'n gwybod bod y Gweinidog, yn ei hymateb, wedi dweud nad yw hi eisiau rhoi gorchmynion i'r byd chwaraeon, ond mae Llywodraeth Cymru, yn y gorffennol, wedi camu i mewn pan fo cyflogaeth mewn perygl. Yn ogystal â chefnogi clybiau, mae'r rhanbarthau hyn yn gyflogwyr. Ar hyn o bryd, amcangyfrifir bod y pedwar rhanbarth yn cyfrannu rhwng £50 miliwn a £55 miliwn i rygbi Cymru. Mae hynny'n llawer o arian. Pan ddywedwch yn eich cynnig heddiw fod angen inni siarad ag URC a rhoi mwy o amser iddynt a'r gweddill i gyd, rwy'n credu bod amser yn brin, Weinidog. Mae mis Rhagfyr yn dod yn gyflym, ac mae angen sicrwydd ar y gweithwyr hynny y bydd ganddynt swydd yn y dyfodol. Felly, nid wyf yn ofni pleidleisio dros ein cynnig heddiw sy'n ceisio eglurder ar fywoliaeth pobl, ac ni fyddaf byth yn ymddiheuro am hynny. Rwy'n credu bod gan y Llywodraeth rôl i gamu i mewn a chymryd rhan—

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I think, Minister, the role we have to play is the same as when Tata was going under. We stepped in to protect jobs. We saw the Welsh Government bringing them to the table, taking action. That's what I want to see from the Welsh Government. Time and time again, when my colleagues have asked questions in this Chamber around what was going on here with the WRU, they did not get a satisfying response. I asked at the end of last term for a statement from you, as the Minister for sport, on the WRU, and we didn't get one. Our constituents are concerned right now about the future of sport, and we have been forced to bring this debate here today to try to get answers for our constituents. There is a transparency question. That is the concern here.

I think we could have worked together. I think we should press pause on the WRU's plans until they can come forward and tell us what the numbers really are. How did they come to this conclusion? What are they trying to hide? I think protecting four regions until we know those answers is vital, and that's why we are saying we need to send a clear signal.

The First Minister, the Prif Weinidog, stood in this Chamber leading a Government debate not long ago, in which he spoke about the power of this Chamber, in a motion that the Welsh Government didn't control, on fair funding, calling for fair funding—a motion similar to ours today—and said that this place can send a clear signal. He said the power of all of us in this room working together and voting together can send a clear example. We could have sent to the WRU today a clear message that this is unacceptable, that players deserve better, fans deserve better, taxpayers deserve better, like the local authorities that could be on the hook for these stadiums.

Back in February, the Deputy First Minister said to this Chamber, to the last Labour Government, 'You simply can't wash your hands of this'. That was, now, a Plaid Minister who said those words—that Government can't wash their hands of this. What did she expect that Government to do? There's the question now: what did she expect? Nothing. She said it on the record that she expected action because she believed that this Chamber and this Government can have a strong voice. That's what we're doing.

In the election campaign, in The Pembrokeshire Herald, I'm sure you all would have read:

'Plaid Cymru Senedd election candidates emphasize call for Scarlets’ survival'.

Plaid Cymru put a press release out during the election saying that they wanted to save the Scarlets. And today, they're saying that their Government can't get involved. [Interruption.] You just stood up and said, 'What do you expect me to do?' Minister. That is what you said. And your party put a press release out saying that you could get involved. That is unacceptable. There is a standard here in which we tell the electorate things and we should honour them—[Interruption.] Minister, every time now. Come on, you've just had eight minutes to speak and two interventions. I'm trying to address the point you were raising, Minister. I'm pointing out that your party called for these actions.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Rwy'n credu, Weinidog, fod y rôl y mae'n rhaid inni ei chwarae yr un fath â phan oedd Tata'n methu. Fe wnaethom gamu i mewn i ddiogelu swyddi. Gwelsom Lywodraeth Cymru yn dod â nhw at y bwrdd, yn gweithredu. Dyna beth yr hoffwn ei weld gan Lywodraeth Cymru. Dro ar ôl tro, pan fo fy nghyd-Aelodau wedi gofyn cwestiynau yn y Siambr hon ynglŷn â'r hyn oedd yn digwydd yma gydag URC, ni chawsant ymateb boddhaol. Gofynnais ar ddiwedd y tymor diwethaf am ddatganiad gennych chi, fel y Gweinidog dros chwaraeon, ar URC, ac ni chawsom un. Mae ein hetholwyr yn pryderu nawr am ddyfodol chwaraeon, a chawsom ein gorfodi i ddod â'r ddadl hon yma heddiw i geisio cael atebion i'n hetholwyr. Mae'n fater o dryloywder. Dyna'r pryder yma.

Rwy'n credu y gallem fod wedi gweithio gyda'n gilydd. Rwy'n credu y dylem bwyso am oedi cynlluniau URC hyd nes y gallant ddweud wrthym beth yw'r ffigurau mewn gwirionedd. Sut y gwnaethant ddod i'r casgliad hwn? Beth y maent yn ceisio ei guddio? Rwy'n credu ei bod hi'n hanfodol diogelu pedwar rhanbarth hyd nes ein bod yn gwybod yr atebion hynny, a dyna pam ein bod ni'n dweud bod angen inni anfon neges glir.

Cododd y Prif Weinidog yn y Siambr hon i arwain dadl gan y Llywodraeth beth amser yn ôl, lle siaradodd am bŵer y Siambr hon, mewn cynnig nad oedd Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei reoli, ar gyllid teg, yn galw am gyllid teg—cynnig tebyg i'n cynnig ni heddiw—a dywedodd y gall y lle hwn anfon neges glir. Dywedodd y gall pŵer pob un ohonom yn yr ystafell hon yn gweithio gyda'n gilydd ac yn pleidleisio gyda'n gilydd anfon esiampl glir. Gallem fod wedi anfon neges glir at URC heddiw fod hyn yn annerbyniol, fod chwaraewyr yn haeddu gwell, cefnogwyr yn haeddu gwell, trethdalwyr yn haeddu gwell, fel yr awdurdodau lleol y gallai fod arian yn ddyledus iddynt am y stadiymau hyn.

Yn ôl ym mis Chwefror, dywedodd y Dirprwy Brif Weinidog wrth y Siambr, wrth y Llywodraeth Lafur ddiwethaf, 'Ni allwch olchi eich dwylo o hyn'. Gweinidog Plaid Cymru bellach a ddywedodd y geiriau hynny—na all y Llywodraeth olchi eu dwylo o hyn. Beth oedd hi'n disgwyl i'r Llywodraeth ei wneud? Dyna'r cwestiwn nawr: beth oedd hi'n ei ddisgwyl? Dim byd. Fe'i cofnodwyd yn dweud ei bod hi'n disgwyl gweld gweithredu'n digwydd oherwydd ei bod yn credu y gall y Siambr hon a'r Llywodraeth hon gael llais cryf. Dyna rydym ni'n ei wneud.

Yn yr ymgyrch etholiadol, yn The Pembrokeshire Herald, rwy'n siŵr y byddwch chi i gyd wedi darllen:

'Mae ymgeiswyr Plaid Cymru yn etholiad y Senedd yn pwysleisio'r alwad i gadw'r Scarlets'.

Cyhoeddodd Plaid Cymru ddatganiad i'r wasg yn ystod yr etholiad yn dweud eu bod am achub y Scarlets. A heddiw, maent yn dweud na all eu Llywodraeth fod yn rhan o'r peth. [Torri ar draws.] Fe wnaethoch chi godi a dweud, 'Beth ydych chi'n disgwyl i mi ei wneud?', Weinidog. Dyna a ddywedoch chi. Ac fe wnaeth eich plaid ryddhau datganiad i'r wasg yn dweud y gallech chi fod yn rhan o'r peth. Mae hynny'n annerbyniol. Mae safon yma lle rydym yn dweud pethau wrth yr etholwyr a dylem eu hanrhydeddu—[Torri ar draws.] Weinidog, bob tro nawr. Dewch, rydych chi newydd gael wyth munud i siarad a dau ymyriad. Rwy'n ceisio mynd i'r afael â'r pwynt roeddech chi'n ei godi, Weinidog. Rwy'n nodi bod eich plaid wedi galw am y camau hyn.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
How? That is the headline under which the party put out a press release there, and today you're saying you can't do anything about it. I think that is an integrity issue right there, absolutely.

Rugby is so much more important, and the WRU have hidden at every opportunity. They've invited Members in this place for a briefing. The briefing wasn't clear and transparent—I sat in it. I've spoken to council leaders that have real concerns about what they could end up with—[Interruption.]—serious money that's going to—. No, Minister, it's not clickbait. When it's real jobs on the line, you'd think you'd actually listen to that. When we see talent leaving Wales now to go and play in English leagues because of the uncertainty here, I think the Government should be listening. That is a concern. Think of the jobs. Think of what we're sending—. The young people that have aspired to play rugby in Wales, looked up at their heroes, and that jersey will no longer exist if the WRU have their way. Heritage gone.

I refuse to stand by and tell my constituents I was not willing to vote for this motion today. I will not tell constituents who have e-mailed telling me about the uncertainty of rugby—I won't be saying, 'I did nothing, I said we were going to let the WRU carry on.' I think we should send a clear signal to them.

To get to the point, the economy relies heavily on these. We've heard from Members like Steven talking about the pub industries. We've heard Carmelo talking about Llanelli in particular. Our economy is struggling in these areas. What the Scarlets and the Ospreys represent, especially the Scarlets in particular, in west Wales, an area that doesn't have a lot of sporting events sent over—. Here in Cardiff, we're quite blessed that there are a lot. We're seeing growing football and rugby in Newport. But in west Wales, it's not so much.

The outreach programmes that the Scarlets are a part of down there help get young people off the streets, get them out from in front of a computer screen. They're a part of the preventative health scheme that we hear this Government talk so much about. But, actually, via this motion here, we could be taking people off the front line that are delivering these services for young people. That's a concern, the wider impact.

Rugby isn't just a sport. Rugby can be a family when you're stood on a terrace, even with opposition fans. It's good for people's mental health. It's a good way of getting out of the house, getting out of the office. For those fans who are e-mailing us on a regular basis, it's a sign of desperation that their lifeline, as they feel, is going away. Their identity could be stripped off them. Why? Because someone called the WRU, the worst-run union right now, won't tell them why their club could be stripped from them, that a competition, a fight between the west must take place. It's unacceptable. You can't treat livelihoods, identities like this.

We've heard from Steve of the Celtic Warriors, when we were promised by the WRU, then, no more restructure, this is it. We've seen the damage it did to Pontypridd and Bridgend, two strong, proud rugby communities no longer there. Are we really prepared to say—
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Sut? Dyna'r pennawd y mae'r blaid wedi cyhoeddi datganiad i'r wasg oddi tano, a heddiw rydych chi'n dweud na allwch chi wneud unrhyw beth am y peth. Rwy'n credu bod cwestiwn ynghylch uniondeb yno, yn bendant.

Mae rygbi gymaint yn bwysicach, ac mae URC wedi cuddio ar bob cyfle. Maent wedi gwahodd Aelodau yn y lle hwn i gyfarfod briffio. Nid oedd y briff yn glir ac yn dryloyw—fe'i mynychais. Rwyf wedi siarad ag arweinwyr cyngor sydd â phryderon gwirioneddol am yr hyn y gallent orfod ei wynebu yn y pen draw—[Torri ar draws.] —arian difrifol sy'n mynd i—. Na, Weinidog, nid abwyd clicio mohono. Pan fo swyddi go iawn yn y fantol, fe fyddech chi'n meddwl y byddech chi'n gwrando ar hynny. Pan welwn dalent yn gadael Cymru nawr i fynd i chwarae yng nghynghreiriau Lloegr oherwydd yr ansicrwydd yma, rwy'n credu y dylai'r Llywodraeth wrando. Mae hynny'n bryder. Meddyliwch am y swyddi. Meddyliwch am yr hyn rydym yn ei anfon—. Y bobl ifanc sydd wedi dyheu am chwarae rygbi yng Nghymru, wedi edrych i fyny ar eu harwyr, ac ni fydd y crys hwnnw'n bodoli mwyach os bydd URC yn cael eu ffordd. Bydd y dreftadaeth honno wedi mynd.

Rwy'n gwrthod camu i'r naill ochr a dweud wrth fy etholwyr nad oeddwn yn fodlon pleidleisio dros y cynnig hwn heddiw. Nid wyf am ddweud wrth etholwyr sydd wedi e-bostio i ddweud wrthyf am ansicrwydd rygbi—ni fyddaf yn dweud, 'Ni wneuthum unrhyw beth, dywedais y byddem yn gadael i URC barhau.' Rwy'n credu y dylem anfon neges glir iddynt.

I wneud y pwynt, mae'r economi'n dibynnu'n helaeth ar y rhain. Clywsom gan Aelodau fel Steven yn siarad am ddiwydiannau tafarndai. Clywsom Carmelo yn siarad am Lanelli yn enwedig. Mae ein heconomi yn ei chael hi'n anodd yn yr ardaloedd hyn. Yr hyn y mae'r Scarlets a'r Gweilch yn ei gynrychioli, yn enwedig y Scarlets yng ngorllewin Cymru, ardal sydd heb lawer o ddigwyddiadau chwaraeon—. Yma yng Nghaerdydd, mae'n fendith fod yna lawer. Rydym yn gweld pêl-droed a rygbi'n tyfu yng Nghasnewydd. Ond nid cymaint yng ngorllewin Cymru.

Mae'r rhaglenni allgymorth y mae'r Scarlets yn rhan ohonynt yn helpu i gael pobl ifanc oddi ar y strydoedd, yn eu cael i ffwrdd oddi wrth sgrin cyfrifiadur. Maent yn rhan o'r cynllun iechyd ataliol y clywn y Llywodraeth hon yn siarad cymaint amdano. Ond mewn gwirionedd, trwy'r cynnig hwn gan URC, gallem fod yn tynnu pobl oddi ar y rheng flaen sy'n darparu'r gwasanaethau hyn i bobl ifanc. Mae hynny'n bryder, yr effaith ehangach.

Nid camp yn unig yw rygbi. Gall rygbi fod yn deulu pan fyddwch chi'n sefyll ar deras, hyd yn oed gyda chefnogwyr y gwrthwynebwyr. Mae'n dda i iechyd meddwl pobl. Mae'n ffordd dda o fynd allan o'r tŷ, mynd allan o'r swyddfa. I'r cefnogwyr sy'n anfon e-byst atom yn rheolaidd, mae'n arwydd o anobaith fod eu rhaff achub, fel y maent yn ei theimlo, yn diflannu. Gallent golli eu hunaniaeth. Pam? Am na wnaiff rhywun o'r enw URC, yr undeb sy'n cael ei redeg waethaf ar hyn o bryd, ddweud wrthynt pam y gallent golli eu clwb, fod rhaid i gystadleuaeth ddigwydd, brwydr rhwng timau'r gorllewin. Mae'n annerbyniol. Ni allwch drin bywoliaeth pobl, hunaniaeth pobl fel hyn.

Clywsom gan Steve am y Rhyfelwyr Celtaidd, pan gawsom addewid gan URC, yna, dim mwy o ailstrwythuro, dyma ni. Gwelsom y niwed a wnaeth i Bontypridd a Phen-y-bont ar Ogwr, dwy gymuned rygbi gref a balch nad ydynt yno mwyach. A ydym ni wir yn barod i ddweud—

Thank you, Llywydd. But on the point, right now, out there, what are we sending to the people of Wales that this place does? With an issue where they step forward and tell us they're concerned about something, that we say, 'It's not our responsibility here.' Government should be oversight. We've heard the case. The taxpayers' money is on the line. That's why we must intervene here. Bring them forward.

Now, Minister, as I said, I tried to ask you for a statement on this. None was brought forward. We were forced to bring the debate. The December deadline is coming. There isn't assurances with the regions now. So, if you are going to vote for your amendment, and you try to stop ours today, and you're going to say you don't support the four and that you're going to let the WRU continue with its unchecks and balances, we'll be back here when the danger comes if you don't support them now, because we know the WRU will push this through. XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Cynnig NDM9313 Llŷr Powell

Cefnogwyd gan Andrew Griffin, John Clark

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn galw ar Lywodraeth Cymru i ailwampio trefniadau trwyddedu tai amlfeddiannaeth a rheolau cymhwysedd tai cymdeithasol i roi terfyn ar allu gwladolion tramor i gael mynediad at Dai Amlfeddiannaeth a thai cymdeithasol, gan gynnwys gweithio gyda Llywodraeth y DU lle bo angen.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Motion NDM9313 Llŷr Powell

Supported by Andrew Griffin, John Clark

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Calls on the Welsh Government to overhaul houses in multiple occupation licensing and social-housing eligibility rules to end access to HMOs and social housing for foreign nationals, including working with the UK Government where necessary.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 8. Reform UK Debate: Access to HMOs and social housing for foreign nationals

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 8. Dadl Reform UK: Mynediad at dai amlfeddiannaeth a thai cymdeithasol i wladolion tramor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 8. Reform UK Debate: Access to HMOs and social housing for foreign nationals
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move the motion tabled in the name of Llŷr Powell. Social housing in Wales is subsidised by public money. It should be reserved for the people of this country, but under this Government, it isn't. Reform UK believes it should be kept for the people of Wales and the United Kingdom. We should be prioritising our own families, our veterans and those who have contributed to our great country. Foreign nationals should not have access to council and social housing, and they should not have access to HMOs that our councils license. If they cannot support themselves, the taxpayer shouldn't be expected to do it for them. We are asking the Welsh Government to change the rules to make that happen and to demand the UK Government acts whenever the law must change in Westminster. 

Let me tell Members of this Chamber and the public what is happening right now. From past experience, I know Plaid and Labour don't like the facts that I bring to this Chamber, but Reform UK believes the people have the right to know. Even when you take out student houses entirely, at the last census five years ago, more than one in four of everyone living in shared private rented accommodation were born outside of the United Kingdom. In Flintshire, it was more than half. In Wrexham, more than half. In Newport, almost half. And sadly, these figures will be much worse today, thanks to the Boris wave of record immigration in the last few years, and the Home Office extending asylum dispersal to every local authority in the country.

HMOs are now the backbone of our deranged asylum system. In Wales, every placement is run by one private contractor. The company is competing directly with Welsh families for housing. Only the other week, landlords in our constituency in Gower and Swansea reached out to me, stating they were contacted by this very company asking to use their properties to home asylum seekers. It is putting our families out of homes. More than 3,000 asylum seekers are now housed in dispersal accommodation, including HMOs across Wales: more than 1,300 in Cardiff, 600 in Swansea and more than 300 in Newport—in normal residential streets in our communities, on our doorstep.

Research into the asylum dispersal across England and Wales found that areas receiving more asylum seekers saw a rise in property crime, theft and burglary. It's true and it's on record. [Interruption.] So, you don't like the facts. [Interruption.] No, it's not. They are the facts. If you don't like the facts, don't listen. The social housing situation, subsidised by taxpayers' money, is just as bad. This summer, my team and I sent freedom of information requests to every council in Wales, asking them how many foreign nationals they house. Let's take Newport, for example. As of this summer, more than one in four people in Newport's temporary accommodation whose nationality was recorded were foreign nationals, and close to 1,000 foreign nationals sit on their housing register. Cardiff is even worse. Of Cardiff's social lettings last year, where nationality was recorded, almost 30 per cent went to foreign nationals: nearly three in 10 new tenancies in our capital city handed to people who were not British citizens. But this is only part of the story because—[Interruption.] Yes.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch, Lywydd. Rwy'n gwneud y cynnig a gyflwynwyd yn enw Llŷr Powell. Mae tai cymdeithasol yng Nghymru yn gymorthdaledig gan arian cyhoeddus. Dylid eu cadw ar gyfer pobl y wlad hon, ond o dan y Llywodraeth hon, nid yw hynny'n digwydd. Mae Reform UK yn credu y dylid eu cadw ar gyfer pobl Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig. Dylem flaenoriaethu ein teuluoedd ein hunain, ein cyn-filwyr a'r rhai sydd wedi cyfrannu at ein gwlad wych. Ni ddylai gwladolion tramor gael mynediad at dai cyngor a thai cymdeithasol, ac ni ddylent gael mynediad at dai amlfeddiannaeth y mae ein cynghorau'n eu trwyddedu. Os na allant gynnal eu hunain, ni ddylid disgwyl i'r trethdalwr wneud hynny drostynt. Gofynnwn i Lywodraeth Cymru newid y rheolau i wneud i hynny ddigwydd ac i fynnu bod Llywodraeth y DU yn gweithredu pryd bynnag y mae'n rhaid i'r gyfraith newid yn San Steffan.

Gadewch imi ddweud wrth Aelodau'r Siambr hon a'r cyhoedd beth sy'n digwydd ar hyn o bryd. O brofiad y gorffennol, rwy'n gwybod nad yw Plaid Cymru a Llafur yn hoffi'r ffeithiau rwy'n eu dwyn i'r Siambr hon, ond mae Reform UK yn credu bod gan y bobl hawl i wybod. Hyd yn oed pan fyddwch chi'n tynnu tai myfyrwyr allan yn gyfan gwbl, yn y cyfrifiad diwethaf bum mlynedd yn ôl, cafodd mwy nag un o bob pedwar o bawb sy'n byw mewn llety rhent preifat a rennir eu geni y tu allan i'r Deyrnas Unedig. Yn sir y Fflint, roedd yn fwy na hanner. Yn Wrecsam, mwy na hanner. Yng Nghasnewydd, bron i hanner. Ac yn anffodus, bydd y ffigurau hyn yn llawer gwaeth heddiw, diolch i don Boris o lefelau mewnfudo uwch nag erioed yn y blynyddoedd diwethaf, a'r Swyddfa Gartref yn ymestyn gwasgariad ceiswyr lloches i bob awdurdod lleol yn y wlad.

Tai amlfeddiannaeth bellach yw asgwrn cefn ein system geiswyr lloches wallgof. Yng Nghymru, caiff pob lleoliad ei redeg gan un contractwr preifat. Mae'r cwmni'n cystadlu'n uniongyrchol â theuluoedd Cymru am dai. Yr wythnos o'r blaen, fe wnaeth landlordiaid yn ein hetholaeth yng Ngŵyr Abertawe estyn allan ataf, gan ddweud bod yr union gwmni hwn wedi cysylltu â nhw i ofyn am gael defnyddio eu heiddo i gartrefu ceiswyr lloches. Mae'n golygu nad oes cartrefi ar gyfer ein teuluoedd ni. Mae mwy na 3,000 o geiswyr lloches bellach mewn llety gwasgaru, gan gynnwys tai amlfeddiannaeth ledled Cymru: mwy na 1,300 yng Nghaerdydd, 600 yn Abertawe a mwy na 300 yng Nghasnewydd—mewn strydoedd preswyl arferol yn ein cymunedau, ar garreg ein drws.

Canfu ymchwil i wasgariad ceiswyr lloches ledled Cymru a Lloegr fod ardaloedd sy'n derbyn mwy o geiswyr lloches wedi gweld cynnydd mewn troseddau eiddo, dwyn a byrgleriaeth. Mae'n wir ac mae wedi'i gofnodi. [Torri ar draws.] Felly, nid ydych chi'n hoffi'r ffeithiau. [Torri ar draws.] Na. Dyna yw'r ffeithiau. Os nad ydych chi'n hoffi'r ffeithiau, peidiwch â gwrando. Mae sefyllfa tai cymdeithasol, a gymorthdelir gan arian trethdalwyr, yr un mor wael. Yr haf hwn, anfonodd fy nhîm a minnau geisiadau rhyddid gwybodaeth at bob cyngor yng Nghymru, gan ofyn iddynt faint o ddinasyddion tramor y maent yn darparu cartref ar eu cyfer. Gadewch inni gymryd Casnewydd, er enghraifft. Yr haf hwn, roedd mwy nag un o bob pedwar o bobl mewn llety dros dro yng Nghasnewydd y cofnodwyd eu cenedligrwydd fel dinasyddion tramor, ac mae bron i 1,000 o wladolion tramor ar eu cofrestr dai. Mae Caerdydd hyd yn oed yn waeth. O'r eiddo cymdeithasol a osodwyd yng Nghaerdydd y llynedd, lle cofnodwyd cenedligrwydd, aeth bron i 30 y cant i ddinasyddion tramor: bron i dair o bob deg tenantiaeth newydd yn ein prifddinas wedi'u trosglwyddo i bobl nad oeddent yn ddinasyddion Prydeinig. Ond dim ond rhan o'r stori yw hyn oherwydd—[Torri ar draws.] Iawn.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Member_job_title_Welsh: Y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Effeithiolrwydd Llywodraeth a’r Cyfansoddiad
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Could I ask you to clarify, are you talking about nationality as self-recorded or are you talking about citizenship and UK passport holders, because there is a difference between both?
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: A gaf i ofyn i chi egluro, a ydych chi'n sôn am genedligrwydd hunangofnodedig neu a ydych chi'n sôn am ddinasyddiaeth a deiliaid pasbortau'r DU, oherwydd mae gwahaniaeth rhwng y ddau?

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 8. Dadl Reform UK: Mynediad at dai amlfeddiannaeth a thai cymdeithasol i wladolion tramor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 8. Reform UK Debate: Access to HMOs and social housing for foreign nationals
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
It's the latter. And like I say, 22 councils—they don't have that data, most of them, and this is of what's actually been recorded. And that was my question: why isn't it recorded? Our taxpayers want to know. So, I'll carry on.

But this is only part of the story, because many councils refused to answer my request, either on the grounds of cost or because they don't record nationality at all, which I just mentioned. So, many of the areas either can't or won't tell the taxpayer the truth. How did we get here?

Allocations in Wales still run on Part VI of the Housing Act 1996. Councils must give reasonable preference to people in housing need. There is nothing in that framework about how long you have lived here, nothing about citizenship. In 2011, England gave its councils the power to decide who qualifies for social housing. Hundreds now apply a residence test in England before anyone joins that list. Wales didn't do the same.

Last December, Wales had the chance to fix it. Section 35 of the Homelessness and Social Housing Allocation (Wales) Bill would have given Welsh councils that same power. It was removed by an amendment tabled by the now Minister who's now responsible for housing, who described social housing as a 'universal resource', which should be accessible by everyone. It is not a universal resource. It is a national resource, and it should belong to the people of this nation.

So, here is what the Welsh Government must do—
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Yr ail. Ac fel rwy'n dweud, 22 o gynghorau—nid yw'r data hwnnw ganddynt, y rhan fwyaf ohonynt, a dyma'r hyn sydd wedi'i gofnodi mewn gwirionedd. A dyna oedd fy nghwestiwn: pam nad yw'n cael ei gofnodi? Mae ein trethdalwyr eisiau gwybod. Felly, fe wnaf barhau.

Ond rhan o'r stori'n unig yw hyn, oherwydd mae llawer o gynghorau wedi gwrthod ateb fy nghais, naill ai ar sail cost neu am nad ydynt yn cofnodi cenedligrwydd o gwbl. Felly, mae llawer o ardaloedd nad ydynt yn gallu, neu nad ydynt am ddweud y gwir wrth y trethdalwr. Sut y gwnaethom gyrraedd yma?

Mae dyraniadau yng Nghymru yn dal i gael eu gweithredu ar Ran VI o Ddeddf Tai 1996. Rhaid i gynghorau roi blaenoriaeth resymol i bobl sydd ag angen o ran tai. Nid oes unrhyw beth yn y fframwaith hwnnw am ba mor hir rydych chi wedi byw yma, dim byd am ddinasyddiaeth. Yn 2011, rhoddodd Lloegr bŵer i'w chynghorau benderfynu pwy sy'n gymwys i gael tai cymdeithasol. Mae cannoedd bellach yn defnyddio prawf preswylio yn Lloegr cyn i unrhyw un fynd ar y rhestr honno. Ni wnaeth Cymru yr un peth.

Fis Rhagfyr diwethaf, cafodd Cymru gyfle i ddatrys hyn. Byddai adran 35 o'r Bil Digartrefedd a Dyrannu Tai Cymdeithasol (Cymru) wedi rhoi'r un pŵer i gynghorau Cymru. Cafodd ei ddileu gan welliant a gyflwynwyd gan y Gweinidog sydd bellach yn gyfrifol am dai, a ddisgrifiodd dai cymdeithasol fel 'adnodd cyffredinol', a ddylai fod yn hygyrch i bawb. Nid yw'n adnodd cyffredinol. Mae'n adnodd cenedlaethol, a dylai berthyn i bobl y genedl hon.

Felly, dyma beth sy'n rhaid i Lywodraeth Cymru ei wneud—

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Absolutely, it's on record, and if that's the best you can come back with, have a little time to think, and I'll take another intervention.

So, first, bring back section 35, legislate to give every Welsh council the power to set qualification rules for its register, and use it to close the register to foreign nationals. Second, amend the allocation of housing and homelessness regulations. Welsh Ministers decide who is eligible. Strip it back to the absolute minimum devolved legislation allows. Third, rewrite the code of guidance and the preference framework so that British citizens with a connection to their communities come first every time. Fourth, houses in multiple occupation. Councils license these properties—wait two ticks, Ken—and Welsh Ministers set the conditions attached to those licences. Every licence holder should be required to verify and record the nationality and immigration status of every occupant, and the use of HMOs across Wales as asylum accommodation must end. Yes, go on.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Yn hollol, mae wedi'i gofnodi, ac os mai dyna'r gorau y gallwch chi ddod yn ôl ag ef, cymerwch ychydig o amser i feddwl, ac fe dderbyniaf ymyriad arall.

Felly, yn gyntaf, dewch ag adran 35 yn ôl, deddfwch i roi pŵer i bob cyngor yng Nghymru osod rheolau cymhwyso ar gyfer ei gofrestr, a defnyddiwch ef i gau'r gofrestr i wladolion tramor. Yn ail, diwygiwch reoliadau dyrannu tai a digartrefedd. Gweinidogion Cymru sy'n penderfynu pwy sy'n gymwys. Torrwch ef yn ôl i'r isafswm absoliwt y mae deddfwriaeth ddatganoledig yn ei ganiatáu. Yn drydydd, ailysgrifennwch y cod canllawiau a'r fframwaith ffafriaeth fel bod dinasyddion Prydeinig sydd â chysylltiad â'u cymunedau yn dod yn gyntaf bob tro. Yn bedwerydd, tai amlfeddiannaeth. Mae cynghorau'n trwyddedu'r eiddo hyn—arhoswch ddwy eiliad, Ken—ac mae Gweinidogion Cymru'n gosod yr amodau sy'n gysylltiedig â'r trwyddedau hynny. Dylid gofyn i bob deiliad trwydded ddilysu a chofnodi cenedligrwydd a statws mewnfudo pob preswylydd, a rhaid dod â'r defnydd o dai amlfeddiannaeth fel llety i geiswyr lloches i ben ledled Cymru. Iawn, ewch amdani.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Well, if you want to—. You talk about political point-scoring. I'll be precise about where this meets the UK law—[Interruption.] No, no. Because that—[Interruption.] Well, you want to political point-score—that's fine, but there we go. Because that is exactly why our motion names the UK Government. Under the Equality Act 2010, nationality is part of the legal framework definition of race. The Act already carries expectations for acts required by immigration law. That is why a landlord in England can lawfully refuse a tenant with no right to rent. So, the UK Government must act. Where bogus equality and human rights laws stand in the way, it must legislate to put British people first.

Reform UK would end access to social housing for foreign nationals, with tenants required to find private accommodation not at the taxpayer's expense. The criteria for occupation of new and existing social housing should be overhauled, with priority given to veterans, our workers, alarm-clock Britain and our most vulnerable. We would overhaul HMO licensing to prevent migrant HMOs. Licences will be refused, revoked or suspended when a landlord is caught knowingly housing illegal immigrants. The people of Wales sent Reform here on a promise to put our own people first for housing. This motion does exactly that, and I urge Members to support this motion.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Wel, os ydych chi eisiau—. Rydych chi'n sôn am sgorio pwyntiau gwleidyddol. Fe fyddaf yn fanwl ynglŷn â ble mae hyn yn cysylltu â chyfraith y DU—[Torri ar draws.] Na na. Oherwydd—[Torri ar draws.] Wel, rydych chi eisiau sgorio pwyntiau gwleidyddol—iawn, ond dyna ni. Oherwydd dyna'n union pam y mae ein cynnig yn enwi Llywodraeth y DU. O dan Ddeddf Cydraddoldeb 2010, mae cenedligrwydd yn rhan o ddiffiniad y fframwaith cyfreithiol o hil. Mae'r Ddeddf eisoes yn cynnwys disgwyliadau ar gyfer gweithredoedd sy'n ofynnol gan gyfraith mewnfudo. Dyna pam y gall landlord yn Lloegr wrthod tenant heb hawl i rentu yn gyfreithlon. Felly, rhaid i Lywodraeth y DU weithredu. Lle mae deddfau cydraddoldeb a hawliau dynol ffug yn sefyll yn y ffordd, rhaid iddi ddeddfu i roi pobl Prydain yn gyntaf.

Byddai Reform UK yn rhoi diwedd ar fynediad at dai cymdeithasol i wladolion tramor, gyda thenantiaid yn gorfod dod o hyd i lety preifat heb fod ar draul y trethdalwr. Dylid ailwampio'r meini prawf ar gyfer meddiannaeth tai cymdeithasol newydd a rhai sy'n bodoli'n barod, gyda blaenoriaeth i gyn-filwyr, ein gweithwyr, Prydain y cloc larwm a'n pobl fwyaf agored i niwed. Byddem yn ailwampio trwyddedu tai amlfeddiannaeth i atal tai amlfeddiannaeth mudwyr. Bydd trwyddedau'n cael eu gwrthod, eu dirymu neu eu hatal pan fydd landlord yn cael ei ddal yn rhoi cartref i fewnfudwyr anghyfreithlon gan wybod ei fod yn gwneud hynny. Anfonodd pobl Cymru Reform yma ar addewid i roi ein pobl ein hunain yn gyntaf o ran tai. Mae'r cynnig hwn yn gwneud yn union hynny, ac rwy'n annog yr Aelodau i'w gefnogi.

Gwelliant 1—Heledd Fychan, Lynne Neagle

Dileu popeth a rhoi yn ei le:

Cynnig bod y Senedd:

1. Yn nodi bod tai cymdeithasol yn cael eu dyrannu gan awdurdodau lleol yn unol â deddfwriaeth a chynlluniau dyrannu lleol, gyda blaenoriaeth yn cael ei phennu yn ôl yr angen am dai a chategorïau blaenoriaeth statudol.

2. Yn cydnabod bod cymhwysedd ar gyfer tai cymdeithasol a chymorth digartrefedd yn cael ei lywodraethu gan ddeddfwriaeth, gan gynnwys darpariaethau sy'n ymwneud â statws mewnfudo a phreswyliad cyfreithlon yn y Deyrnas Unedig.

3. Yn credu bod penderfyniadau sy'n ymwneud â thrwyddedu a rheoli tai amlfeddiannaeth yn cael eu gwneud orau gan awdurdodau lleol o fewn y fframwaith a sefydlwyd gan ddeddfwriaeth a chanllawiau Llywodraeth Cymru.

4. Yn nodi bod penderfyniadau ynghylch gwasgariad a llety pobl sy'n ceisio lloches yn cael eu cadw i Lywodraeth y DU ac yn credu y dylai trefniadau gwasgaru effeithiol ystyried capasiti lleol, effaith debygol ar gydlyniant cymunedol a’r gwasanaethau cymorth sydd ar gael.

5. Yn cefnogi ymgysylltu rhwng Llywodraeth Cymru a Llywodraeth y DU i hyrwyddo trefniadau gwasgaru teg a chynaliadwy ac i gefnogi integreiddio a chydlyniant cymunedol llwyddiannus ledled Cymru.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Amendment 1—Heledd Fychan, Lynne Neagle

Delete all and replace with:

To propose that the Senedd:

1. Notes social housing is allocated by local authorities in accordance with legislation and local allocation schemes, with priority determined by housing need and statutory priority categories.

2. Recognises eligibility for social housing and homelessness assistance is governed by legislation, including provisions relating to immigration status and lawful residence in the United Kingdom.

3. Believes decisions relating to the licensing and management of houses in multiple occupation are best taken by local authorities within the framework established by legislation and Welsh Government guidance.

4. Notes decisions regarding the dispersal of and accommodation for people seeking asylum are reserved to the UK Government and believes that effective dispersal arrangements should take account of local capacity, likely impact on community cohesion and the availability of support services.

5. Supports engagement between the Welsh Government and the UK Government to promote fair and sustainable dispersal arrangements and to support successful integration and community cohesion across Wales.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 8. Dadl Reform UK: Mynediad at dai amlfeddiannaeth a thai cymdeithasol i wladolion tramor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 8. Reform UK Debate: Access to HMOs and social housing for foreign nationals
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move the Conservative amendment in the name of Paul Davies.

Now, there is no doubt that people across Wales are concerned about pressure on housing. They see growing waiting lists, rising rents and increasing difficulty for local people to access affordable homes. They expect politicians to take those concerns seriously and to offer practical solutions. Unfortunately, what we have before us from Reform today is not a serious attempt to solve a problem. As usual, it is a headline-grabbing motion that falls apart the moment you examine how it would work in actual fact. We believe—the Conservative Party believes—that social housing must prioritise those with a genuine and established connection to our country. We also agree that accommodation should not be provided to people who are here unlawfully. That is why we have tabled an amendment that takes a practical and deliverable approach and a position that is shared by the UK Conservative Party. What we do not support is a policy so carelessly drafted that it would sweep up people who are legally entitled to be here, legally entitled to work here and legally entitled to housing support under existing arrangements.

The reality is that Reform's motion would not just affect the groups they want to talk about. It would affect foreign students renting rooms in HMOs while studying at Welsh universities, it would affect workers who have come here legally, and it would affect Irish citizens whose rights are protected under the common travel area. Most significantly, it would also affect EU citizens who were given settled status after Brexit. These are people who were explicitly told that there would be no change to their rights if they were already lawfully resident in the United Kingdom. Those commitments were written into the withdrawal agreement and form part of our international obligations. So, Reform need to answer a simple question: are they really proposing that the United Kingdom should tear up agreements it freely entered into, creating uncertainty for British citizens living abroad and risk retaliatory action from our European neighbours, all to pursue a policy they have no realistic route in implementing? That is the logical consequence of what they are proposing.

Now, many of the very people now championing this motion were enthusiastic supporters of the 'leave' campaign, which repeatedly assured EU citizens already living here that their rights would be protected. Back then, they said one thing; today, they are saying another. So, which position is right? We believe in controlled immigration, secure borders and fairness in the allocation of public services. But we also believe that promises made should be promises kept. That is why our amendment takes a different path. We call for reform of social housing eligibility rules where needed, while protecting the rights of British and Irish citizens and those covered by the withdrawal agreement. We call for action against the use of HMOs to accommodate those who are unlawfully present in the United Kingdom, including those who have arrived illegally. Those are measures that can actually be implemented—they are legally sound, they are proportionate and they address legitimate public concerns without descending into gesture politics.

We should also be clear that Welsh Government cannot escape responsibility. Labour have overseen years of pressure on housing supply, years of failure to deliver the homes that Wales needs, and years of inaction when local authorities and communities have raised concerns about housing availability. So, while Reform offer slogans, Labour try to defend their record and Plaid set out their next 100 days of uncosted aims, the Welsh Conservatives are offering solutions—solutions that recognise the pressure on housing, uphold the rule of law and can actually be delivered. For those reasons, Members should reject Reform's flawed motion and support ours. Thank you.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Diolch, Lywydd. Rwy'n cynnig gwelliant y Ceidwadwyr yn enw Paul Davies.

Nawr, nid oes unrhyw amheuaeth fod pobl ledled Cymru yn poeni am bwysau o ran tai. Maent yn gweld rhestrau aros cynyddol, rhenti cynyddol ac anhawster cynyddol i bobl leol gael mynediad at gartrefi fforddiadwy. Maent yn disgwyl i wleidyddion roi ystyriaeth ddifrifol i'r pryderon hynny ac i gynnig atebion ymarferol. Yn anffodus, nid yw'r hyn sydd gennym o'n blaenau gan Reform heddiw yn ymgais ddifrifol i ddatrys problem. Fel arfer, mae'n gynnig i fachu penawdau sy'n chwalu yr eiliad y byddwch chi'n archwilio sut y byddai'n gweithio mewn gwirionedd. Rydym ni'n credu—mae'r Blaid Geidwadol yn credu—fod rhaid i dai cymdeithasol flaenoriaethu'r rhai sydd â chysylltiad dilys a sefydledig â'n gwlad. Rydym hefyd yn cytuno na ddylid darparu llety i bobl sydd yma yn anghyfreithlon. Dyna pam ein bod wedi cyflwyno gwelliant sy'n arfer dull ymarferol a chyflawnadwy o weithredu a safbwynt sy'n cael ei rannu gan Blaid Geidwadol y DU. Yr hyn nad ydym yn ei gefnogi yw polisi sydd wedi'i ddrafftio mor ddiofal fel y byddai'n cynnwys pobl sydd â hawl gyfreithiol i fod yma, pobl sydd â hawl gyfreithiol i weithio yma a hawl gyfreithiol i gymorth tai o dan y trefniadau presennol.

Y gwir amdani yw nad y grwpiau y maent hwy'n siarad amdanynt yn unig fyddai cynnig Reform yn effeithio arnynt. Byddai'n effeithio ar fyfyrwyr tramor sy'n rhentu ystafelloedd mewn tai amlfeddiannaeth wrth iddynt astudio mewn prifysgolion yng Nghymru, byddai'n effeithio ar weithwyr sydd wedi dod yma'n gyfreithlon, a byddai'n effeithio ar ddinasyddion Iwerddon y mae eu hawliau wedi'u diogelu o dan yr ardal deithio gyffredin. Yn fwyaf arwyddocaol, byddai hefyd yn effeithio ar ddinasyddion yr UE y rhoddwyd statws preswylwyr sefydlog iddynt ar ôl Brexit. Mae'r rhain yn bobl y dywedwyd wrthynt yn glir na fyddai unrhyw newid i'w hawliau os oeddent eisoes yn preswylio'n gyfreithlon yn y Deyrnas Unedig. Ysgrifennwyd yr ymrwymiadau hynny yn y cytundeb ymadael ac maent yn rhan o'n rhwymedigaethau rhyngwladol. Felly, mae angen i Reform ateb cwestiwn syml: a ydynt o ddifrif yn cynnig y dylai'r Deyrnas Unedig rwygo cytundebau yr ymrwymodd iddynt o'i gwirfodd, a chreu ansicrwydd i ddinasyddion Prydain sy'n byw dramor a risg o ddial gan ein cymdogion Ewropeaidd, a'r cyfan er mwyn dilyn polisi nad oes ganddynt lwybr realistig tuag at ei weithredu? Dyna ganlyniad rhesymegol yr hyn y maent yn ei gynnig.

Nawr, roedd llawer o'r union bobl sydd bellach yn hyrwyddo'r cynnig hwn yn gefnogwyr brwdfrydig i'r ymgyrch dros adael a sicrhaodd ddinasyddion yr UE a oedd eisoes yn byw yma dro ar ôl tro y byddai eu hawliau'n cael eu diogelu. Bryd hynny, roeddent yn dweud un peth; heddiw, maent yn dweud rhywbeth arall. Felly, pa safbwynt sy'n gywir? Rydym yn credu mewn mewnfudo dan reolaeth, ffiniau diogel a thegwch wrth ddyrannu gwasanaethau cyhoeddus. Ond credwn hefyd y dylai addewidion a wnaed fod yn addewidion a gedwir. Dyna pam y mae ein gwelliant ni'n dilyn llwybr gwahanol. Rydym yn galw am ddiwygio rheolau cymhwyso ar gyfer tai cymdeithasol lle bo angen, tra'n diogelu hawliau dinasyddion Prydain ac Iwerddon a'r rhai a gwmpesir gan y cytundeb ymadael. Rydym yn galw am weithredu yn erbyn y defnydd o dai amlfeddiannaeth i letya rhai sy'n bresennol yn anghyfreithlon yn y Deyrnas Unedig, gan gynnwys y rhai sydd wedi cyrraedd yn anghyfreithlon. Mae'r rhain yn fesurau y gellir eu gweithredu—maent yn gyfreithiol gadarn, maent yn gymesur ac maent yn mynd i'r afael â phryderon cyhoeddus dilys heb ymroi i wleidyddiaeth ystumiau.

Dylem fod yn glir hefyd na all Llywodraeth Cymru ddianc rhag cyfrifoldeb. Mae Llafur wedi goruchwylio dros flynyddoedd o bwysau ar y cyflenwad tai, blynyddoedd o fethiant i ddarparu'r cartrefi sydd eu hangen ar Gymru, a blynyddoedd o ddiffyg gweithredu pan fo awdurdodau lleol a chymunedau wedi codi pryderon am argaeledd tai. Felly, tra bod Reform yn cynnig sloganau, Llafur yn ceisio amddiffyn eu cyflawniad a Phlaid Cymru'n nodi eu 100 diwrnod nesaf o nodau heb eu costio, mae'r Ceidwadwyr Cymreig yn cynnig atebion—atebion sy'n cydnabod y pwysau ar y cyflenwad tai, sy'n cynnal rheolaeth y gyfraith ac sy'n gyflawnadwy mewn gwirionedd. Am y rhesymau hynny, dylai'r Aelodau wrthod cynnig diffygiol Reform a chefnogi ein cynnig ni. Diolch.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 8. Dadl Reform UK: Mynediad at dai amlfeddiannaeth a thai cymdeithasol i wladolion tramor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 8. Reform UK Debate: Access to HMOs and social housing for foreign nationals

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_welsh: 8. Dadl Reform UK: Mynediad at dai amlfeddiannaeth a thai cymdeithasol i wladolion tramor
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.Agenda_item_english: 8. Reform UK Debate: Access to HMOs and social housing for foreign nationals
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
I'd like to start by declaring an interest as a recent tenant in the private rental sector. Hopefully, this makes it clear from the outset where my priorities lie, because my priority lies with people who need a home, not people who profit from other people's basic need for shelter—and I'm not sure the same can be said about the party opposite on that. However, Nigel Farage's Welsh branch have identified a genuine problem: Wales does not have enough affordable housing. But, once again, they are taking a genuine problem and looking for someone to blame. People who arrive here illegally, asylum seekers and migrants on student or work visas are not eligible for social housing. According to census data, there are an estimated 28,000 non-UK-born people living in social housing in Wales. Meanwhile, an estimated 170,000 people are waiting for social housing in Wales.

The housing crisis is way bigger than the question of migration. Even if the party opposite got their disturbed dream of making 28,000 people homeless, it would not begin to tackle the problem. And this is the only answer they have got: scapegoating migrants. The Reform UK Wales manifesto does not even commit to building a single council or social home. Not one. Not a commitment to a single one. They have no plan to ensure the adequate supply of social housing for everyone, whereas this Plaid Cymru Government is getting on with their commitment to build 20,000 social homes.

The only plan Reform do have, actually, would make the problem worse. Thatcher's right to buy decimated the supply of council homes in the UK, and the Conservatives' right to buy in the 2010s—which many of them will remember as they were members of the party at the time—contributed massively to the UK housing crisis. More than 40 per cent of homes that were sold under that scheme are now in the private rental sector. So, it is laughable that a party advocating for right to buy is complaining about HMOs in Wales, because right to buy would actually increase the number of HMOs in Wales.

And take this in—I won't say it often—Reform is right: there are issues with HMOs. But they have not identified the right issue. Houses in multiple occupation too often result in overcrowding and poor living conditions, while generating profits for the wealthy from this poor standard of living. Instead of asking, 'What kind of home does someone need to thrive?', the market asks, 'What is the minimum amount of private space that someone will pay for?' It is exploitative. We will not solve this housing crisis by making people live more densely on top of each other inside existing homes. I'm not objecting to shared living, because students or friends may genuinely choose it—I've been in that situation myself many times—but too often, with HMOs, economic necessity is masquerading as consumer choice. When someone is living in a bedroom in subdivided housing simply because they cannot afford anything else, that's a housing crisis. Why should people with money get proper homes to live in, but people without money get a bedroom in a subdivided house? Reform UK are on the record complaining about HMOs, but would Reform UK be willing to take on the landlord lobby and reduce the number of legal rooms in HMOs, or strengthen tenants' rights, or end no-fault evictions? What do you think? Because the Reform 2024 manifesto wanted to abolish the Renters' Rights Bill, which set out to end no-fault evictions and strengthen renters' rights, and it will be really interesting to see how they vote on the package of renters' rights that this Welsh Government wants to bring through.

So, to summarise, Reform don't want people born outside the UK to access social housing, but they also don't want them to access HMOs. Their manifesto means they're clearly not interested in building social housing and, through right to buy, they actually support decreasing the supply of council housing, which will increase dependence on the private rental sector and increase the number of HMOs that they want to see fewer of, but they aren't planning on building social or council homes as an alternative and actually support selling them off, remember. Does that make any sense to anyone here? No, it doesn't. But at least one thing is clear from Reform's motion today—Reform don't like people born outside the UK—. Sorry, Llywydd, let me correct that. Reform don't want people born outside the UK in social housing or private HMOs in Wales. Diolch yn fawr.
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated:
Hoffwn ddechrau trwy ddatgan buddiant fel tenant diweddar yn y sector rhentu preifat. Gobeithio bod hyn yn ei gwneud hi'n glir o'r dechrau ble mae fy mlaenoriaethau, oherwydd fy mlaenoriaeth yw'r bobl sydd angen cartref, nid pobl sy'n elwa o angen sylfaenol pobl eraill am loches—ac nid wyf yn siŵr y gellir dweud yr un peth am y blaid gyferbyn ar hynny. Fodd bynnag, mae cangen Cymru Nigel Farage wedi nodi problem wirioneddol: nid oes gan Gymru ddigon o dai fforddiadwy. Ond unwaith eto, maent yn cymryd problem go iawn ac yn chwilio am rywun i'w feio. Nid yw pobl sy'n cyrraedd yma'n anghyfreithlon, ceiswyr lloches ac ymfudwyr ar fisâu myfyrwyr neu waith yn gymwys i gael tai cymdeithasol. Yn ôl data'r cyfrifiad, amcangyfrifir bod 28,000 o bobl nad ydynt wedi'u geni yn y DU yn byw mewn tai cymdeithasol yng Nghymru. Yn y cyfamser, amcangyfrifir bod 170,000 o bobl yn aros am dai cymdeithasol yng Nghymru.

Mae'r argyfwng tai yn llawer mwy na chwestiwn mudo. Hyd yn oed pe bai'r blaid gyferbyn yn cael eu breuddwyd ynfyd o wneud 28,000 o bobl yn ddigartref, ni fyddai'n dechrau mynd i'r afael â'r broblem. A dyma'r unig ateb sydd ganddynt: gwneud ymfudwyr yn fychod dihangol. Nid yw maniffesto Reform UK Cymru yn ymrwymo i adeiladu un cartref cyngor neu gartref cymdeithasol hyd yn oed. Dim un. Ni cheir ymrwymiad i un. Nid oes ganddynt gynllun i sicrhau cyflenwad digonol o dai cymdeithasol i bawb, tra bod Llywodraeth Plaid Cymru yn parhau â'u hymrwymiad i adeiladu 20,000 o gartrefi cymdeithasol.

Byddai'r unig gynllun sydd gan Reform mewn gwirionedd yn gwneud y broblem yn waeth. Fe wnaeth hawl i brynu Thatcher ddinistrio'r cyflenwad o gartrefi cyngor yn y DU, a chyfrannodd hawl i brynu'r Ceidwadwyr yn y 2010au—y bydd llawer ohonynt hwy'n ei gofio gan eu bod yn aelodau o'r blaid honno ar y pryd—yn enfawr at argyfwng tai y DU. Mae mwy na 40 y cant o'r cartrefi a werthwyd o dan y cynllun hwnnw bellach yn y sector rhentu preifat. Felly, mae'n chwerthinllyd fod plaid sy'n cefnogi'r hawl i brynu yn cwyno am dai amlfeddiannaeth yng Nghymru, gan y byddai'r hawl i brynu yn cynyddu nifer y tai amlfeddiannaeth yng Nghymru mewn gwirionedd.

A chlywch hyn—ni fyddaf yn ei ddweud yn aml—mae Reform yn iawn: mae yna broblemau gyda thai amlfeddiannaeth. Ond nid ydynt wedi nodi'r broblem gywir. Mae tai amlfeddiannaeth yn rhy aml yn arwain at orlenwi ac amodau byw gwael, tra'n cynhyrchu elw i'r cyfoethog o'r safon byw wael hon. Yn hytrach na gofyn, 'Pa fath o gartref sydd ei angen ar rywun i ffynnu?', mae'r farchnad yn gofyn, 'Beth yw'r lleiafswm o le preifat y bydd rhywun yn talu amdano?' Mae'n ecsbloetiol. Ni wnawn ddatrys yr argyfwng tai trwy wneud i bobl fyw mewn niferoedd mwy dwys ar ben ei gilydd mewn cartrefi sydd eisoes yn bodoli. Nid wyf yn gwrthwynebu rhannu lle byw, oherwydd gall myfyrwyr neu ffrindiau ei ddewis—rwyf wedi bod yn y sefyllfa honno fy hun sawl gwaith—ond yn rhy aml, gyda thai amlfeddiannaeth, mae angen economaidd yn ffugio bod yn ddewis i ddefnyddwyr. Pan fydd rhywun yn byw mewn ystafell wely mewn tŷ wedi'i isrannu am na allant fforddio unrhyw beth arall, mae hynny'n argyfwng tai. Pam y dylai pobl sydd ag arian gael cartrefi priodol i fyw ynddynt, ond bod pobl heb arian yn cael ystafell wely mewn tŷ wedi'i isrannu? Cofnodwyd Reform UK yn cwyno am dai amlfeddiannaeth, ond a fyddai Reform UK yn fodlon mynd benben â'r lobi landlordiaid a lleihau nifer yr ystafelloedd cyfreithiol mewn tai amlfeddiannaeth, neu gryfhau hawliau tenantiaid, neu roi diwedd ar droi allan heb fai? Tybed? Oherwydd roedd maniffesto Reform 2024 eisiau diddymu'r Bil Hawliau Rhentwyr, a oedd yn ceisio rhoi diwedd ar droi allan heb fai a chryfhau hawliau rhentwyr, a bydd yn ddiddorol iawn gweld sut y maent yn pleidleisio ar y pecyn o hawliau rhentwyr y mae'r Llywodraeth hon eisiau ei gyflwyno.

Felly, i grynhoi, nid yw Reform eisiau i bobl a anwyd y tu allan i'r DU gael tai cymdeithasol, ond nid ydynt eisiau iddynt gael lle mewn tai amlfeddiannaeth chwaith. Mae eu maniffesto'n golygu nad oes ganddynt ddiddordeb mewn adeiladu tai cymdeithasol a thrwy hawl i brynu, maent yn cefnogi lleihau'r cyflenwad o dai cyngor, a fydd yn cynyddu dibyniaeth ar y sector rhentu preifat ac yn cynyddu nifer y tai amlfeddiannaeth y maent am weld llai ohonynt, ond nid ydynt yn bwriadu adeiladu cartrefi cymdeithasol neu gartrefi cyngor fel dewis amgen ac mewn gwirionedd, maent yn cefnogi eu gwerthu, cofiwch. A yw hynny'n gwneud unrhyw synnwyr i unrhyw un yma? Nac ydy. Ond mae o leiaf un peth yn glir yng nghynnig Reform heddiw—nid yw Reform yn hoffi pobl a anwyd y tu allan i'r DU—. Mae'n ddrwg gennyf, Lywydd, gadewch imi gywiro hynny. Nid yw Reform eisiau pobl a anwyd y tu allan i'r DU mewn tai cymdeithasol neu dai amlfeddiannaeth preifat yng Nghymru. Diolch yn fawr.
